The passage proceeds decade by decade: 1940s → 1950s → late 1950s → 1960s-70s → today. This is CHRONOLOGICAL structure, and the thread connecting all periods is increasing abstraction. B is correct. A (comparison) requires side-by-side contrast of languages. C (problem-solution) would require identifying a problem and proposing a solution. D (classification) would organize by type without the temporal progression.

examples.q:
Passage: 'The Roman Republic and the United States share a similar constitutional architecture: both divided power among executive, legislative, and judicial functions to prevent tyranny. However, the Roman system concentrated executive power in two annually elected consuls who could veto each other, while the American system distributes executive power in a single president. Where Rome used a Senate of hereditary aristocrats, America used an elected Senate. The Roman system ultimately proved unstable and collapsed into empire; the American system has so far endured for nearly two and a half centuries.'

Which best describes the overall structure?
opts: A chronological account of both democratic systems
A comparison of the Roman Republic and the United States across shared structural features and key differences
A problem-solution analysis of what caused the fall of the Roman Republic
A description of how the Roman Republic influenced the American founding
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) A comparison of the Roman Republic and the United States across shared structural features and key differences

The passage explicitly compares the two systems: begins with similarity ('similar constitutional architecture'), then contrasts specific elements (consuls vs. president, hereditary vs. elected Senate, stability vs. collapse). Signal words: 'however,' 'while,' 'where.' B accurately identifies the COMPARE/CONTRAST structure. A is wrong — no time progression through events. C is wrong — the fall of Rome is mentioned as an outcome, not the focus. D is wrong — influence is not what's being analyzed.

examples.q:
Passage: 'Antibiotic resistance now kills approximately 700,000 people annually, and without intervention, this toll could reach 10 million per year by 2050. The primary drivers are overprescription in medical settings, routine prophylactic use in agriculture, and patients failing to complete treatment courses. Addressing this crisis will require coordinated action: stewardship programs that restrict antibiotic prescription to confirmed bacterial infections, phasing out agricultural use except for treating illness, and global investment in developing new antibiotic classes.'

The overall structure of this passage is best described as
opts: A chronological history of antibiotic development and resistance
A comparison between medical and agricultural contributions to antibiotic resistance
A presentation of a serious public health problem, its causes, and proposed solutions
A classification of the different types of antibiotic-resistant bacteria
examples.a:
Correct answer: C) A presentation of a serious public health problem, its causes, and proposed solutions

Explicit structure: problem (700,000 deaths, 10M projected) → causes (overprescription, agriculture, incomplete treatment) → solutions (stewardship, agricultural phase-out, new antibiotics). C is correct. A has no chronological progression through time. B partially fits (medical vs. agricultural causes are mentioned) but 'comparison' misses the problem-solution arc. D is wrong — no classification of bacteria types.

examples.q:
Passage: 'Proponents of free trade argue that it increases efficiency, lowers consumer prices, and raises global living standards through comparative advantage. Critics counter that free trade destroys manufacturing employment in wealthier nations and exploits workers in developing ones. Advocates respond that adjustment programs can address displacement while preserving the gains. Skeptics rejoin that adjustment assistance has historically been underfunded and workers rarely recovered their previous incomes.'

The structure is best described as
opts: A chronological account of international trade policy
A classification of different types of economic agreements
A series of alternating claims and counterclaims about free trade policy
A description of how free trade works and its effects on global markets
examples.a:
Correct answer: C) A series of alternating claims and counterclaims about free trade policy

The passage ALTERNATES: proponents → critics → advocates respond → skeptics rejoin. This is classic CLAIM AND COUNTERCLAIM structure. C is correct. A is wrong — no time progression. B is wrong — no categorization of trade types. D is wrong — the passage is about the policy debate, not a neutral description of how free trade works.

examples.q:
Passage: 'Clouds are classified by both altitude and form. High clouds (above 20,000 feet) include cirrus, which are wispy and ice-crystal-based. Middle clouds (6,500–20,000 feet) include altostratus, which appear as a gray sheet, and altocumulus, which form rounded masses. Low clouds include stratus, which form uniform flat layers, and cumulus, which develop vertical mass from updrafts. Cumulonimbus clouds span all altitude levels and are associated with thunderstorms.'

The overall structure of this passage is best described as
opts: A chronological account of cloud formation and dissipation
A comparison of dangerous and non-dangerous cloud types
A hierarchical classification of cloud types by altitude and form
A problem-solution analysis of how clouds affect weather patterns
examples.a:
Correct answer: C) A hierarchical classification of cloud types by altitude and form

The passage CLASSIFIES clouds by two criteria: altitude (high/middle/low) and form (cirrus, stratus, cumulus, etc.), defining each type and its characteristics. C (hierarchical classification) is correct. A is wrong — no time progression. B is wrong — no danger/non-danger comparison. D is wrong — no problem-solution framing.

sessions.title: How Structure Supports Argument
theory: Beyond identifying WHAT the structure is, advanced SAT questions ask WHY the author chose that structure — how the organizational choices SUPPORT the argument being made. These questions might ask: 'Why does the author begin with X before moving to Y?' or 'What is the effect of presenting the counterargument before the main claim?' Understanding the RHETORICAL PURPOSE of structural choices requires you to think about what the author ACHIEVES by organizing the passage as they did.

Common rhetorical effects of structural choices: (1) ACKNOWLEDGING A COUNTERARGUMENT before presenting your own strengthens credibility by showing you have considered other views. (2) PRESENTING BACKGROUND BEFORE ARGUMENT establishes context that makes the argument more compelling or understandable. (3) MOVING FROM SPECIFIC EXAMPLE TO GENERAL PRINCIPLE (or vice versa) builds the argument inductively or deductively. (4) ENDING WITH A CALL TO ACTION or recommendation signals that the author's purpose is persuasive. (5) USING PARALLEL STRUCTURE (presenting multiple items the same way) creates emphasis and makes comparisons clearer.

For these questions, the answer must do two things: accurately describe WHAT the structural move is AND correctly identify WHY it serves the argument. A common trap: answers that correctly describe what a section does but misidentify its PURPOSE. Another trap: answers that correctly state a purpose but inaccurately describe what actually happens in the text. Always check both components of the answer.
keys: Counterargument first = strengthens credibility by showing awareness of other views
Background before argument = establishes context for the argument
Specific → General = inductive reasoning (builds up to a principle)
General → Specific = deductive reasoning (applies a principle to examples)
Parallel structure = creates emphasis and clarity in comparisons
Call to action at end = signals persuasive intent
Check BOTH: what the structural move IS and what it ACHIEVES

examples.q:
Passage structure: 'Many assume that raising the minimum wage primarily helps low-income workers. In fact, research shows that the majority of minimum wage earners are not in households below the poverty line — many are secondary earners in middle-income families. [The passage then argues for more targeted anti-poverty interventions.]'

Why does the author begin by presenting the common assumption before challenging it?
opts: To concede that the common assumption is correct
To establish what the argument is pushing against, making the subsequent evidence more impactful by contrast with what readers likely believe
To prove that minimum wage workers are not poor
To introduce the topic of poverty policy in general
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) To establish what the argument is pushing against, making the subsequent evidence more impactful by contrast with what readers likely believe

Opening with the assumption (what readers likely believe) and then challenging it creates a SETUP-AND-CHALLENGE structure. The surprise of having a common belief overturned makes the evidence more memorable and impactful. B captures this rhetorical function. A says the author concedes (wrong — the author challenges). C misidentifies the purpose as proving a single claim. D is too broad.

examples.q:
Passage structure: [Para 1: Describes a specific case — a fishing community in Indonesia whose livelihoods collapsed after coral reef bleaching.] [Para 2: Shows that 500 million people worldwide depend on coral reefs for food and income.] [Para 3: Argues for international funding to protect coral reefs as a global economic and humanitarian priority.]

What is the effect of beginning with the Indonesian community before presenting the global statistics?
opts: It proves that Indonesia is more affected than other countries
Opening with a specific human case creates emotional engagement that makes readers more receptive to the subsequent global statistics and policy argument
The specific case contradicts the global statistics presented in Para 2
It introduces an exception to the argument made in Para 3
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) Opening with a specific human case creates emotional engagement that makes readers more receptive to the subsequent global statistics and policy argument

This is the classic SPECIFIC → GENERAL structure. The Indonesian case makes the abstract problem concrete and emotionally resonant before the scale is established (500 million). B is correct — emotional engagement is the rhetorical function. A is wrong — no comparison with other countries is implied. C and D are wrong — the specific case supports, not contradicts, the broader argument.

examples.q:
A student argues that nuclear energy should be reconsidered for climate change. The student uses this structure: [Para 1: New technology X was feared as dangerous and economically unviable when introduced.] [Para 2: Regulation and engineering advances made technology X safe and economical.] [Para 3: Nuclear energy is currently viewed the same way X was — as too dangerous and costly.] [Para 4: Argues nuclear could similarly become viable with the right investment.]

What is the rhetorical function of the historical analogy (Paras 1-2)?
opts: To prove that nuclear energy is already safe
To establish a precedent showing that feared technologies can become viable through investment — making the nuclear argument feel consistent with historical pattern rather than utopian
To demonstrate that all new technologies are initially opposed
To provide evidence that nuclear energy's risks have been exaggerated
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) To establish a precedent showing that feared technologies can become viable through investment — making the nuclear argument feel consistent with historical pattern rather than utopian

Historical analogies function to establish PRECEDENT — showing that the proposed development has happened before in analogous circumstances. This makes the argument feel less radical. B is correct. A is wrong — the analogy is about technology X, not nuclear energy directly. C overgeneralizes. D makes a specific claim about nuclear risk that the analogy doesn't directly support.

examples.t: Example 4 — Why Save the Solution for Last
examples.q:
Passage structure: [Para 1: Describes the severity of urban food deserts.] [Para 2: Explains why conventional grocery stores don't enter these neighborhoods (low profit margins).] [Para 3: Documents the health consequences.] [Para 4: Proposes mobile markets and community-owned cooperatives as solutions.]

Why does the author place the proposed solutions (Para 4) after the cause analysis (Para 2) rather than introducing them in Para 1?
opts: The author doesn't know the solutions until the problem is fully analyzed

By establishing the structural CAUSE of food deserts (low profit margins) before the solutions, the author ensures readers understand why solutions must address economic incentives, not just physical access
The solutions are less important than the health consequences
Para 1 is too short to contain both the problem and the solutions
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) By establishing the structural CAUSE of food deserts (low profit margins) before the solutions, the author ensures readers understand why solutions must address economic incentives, not just physical access

The ordering is deliberate: if readers understand WHY food deserts exist (economic — low margins), they'll understand why the solutions (cooperatives that change the economic model) address the root cause. B is correct. A is naive. C reverses the importance hierarchy (the author clearly values the solutions — they form the conclusion). D is a mechanical observation that misses the rhetorical logic.

examples.q:
Passage: 'The candidate's record shows a consistent pattern: she voted to cut education funding when districts needed support; she voted to expand tax incentives when corporations sought relief; she voted to weaken environmental protections when industry requested flexibility.'

What is the rhetorical effect of the parallel 'she voted to...' structure?
opts: It proves the candidate is corrupt

The parallel structure creates emphasis through repetition — the similar grammatical form for three different policy areas reinforces the author's claim of a consistent pattern by making the pattern visually and rhythmically apparent
It introduces a chronological account of her voting record
It provides three separate arguments, each of which can stand independently
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) The parallel structure creates emphasis through repetition — the similar grammatical form for three different policy areas reinforces the author's claim of a consistent pattern by making the pattern visually and rhythmically apparent

PARALLEL STRUCTURE's rhetorical function is EMPHASIS THROUGH REPETITION. The three parallel 'she voted to X when Y needed Z' clauses don't just present facts — their identical form makes the PATTERN feel inevitable and undeniable. B is correct. A adds a corruption inference not made. C is wrong (no chronological order). D is wrong — they work together as a unified argument for a pattern, not independently.

sessions.title: Author's Purpose — Why Was This Written?
theory: Author's Purpose questions ask WHY the author wrote the passage — what they are trying to accomplish. The question stems are: 'Which choice best describes the overall purpose of the text?' or 'What is the main purpose of the passage?' There are six core purposes on the SAT: (1) INFORM/EXPLAIN — present factual information, describe how something works; (2) PERSUADE/ARGUE — advocate for a position, change the reader's mind; (3) ANALYZE/CRITIQUE — examine a topic critically, evaluate strengths and weaknesses; (4) DESCRIBE — create a vivid picture of a scene, person, or object (common in literary excerpts); (5) COUNTER — challenge an existing assumption, claim, or argument; (6) SYNTHESIZE — combine perspectives or evidence to reach a conclusion.

The critical skill is distinguishing between purposes that look similar. INFORM vs. ARGUE: an informative passage presents facts without taking sides; an argumentative passage takes a clear position and marshals evidence for it. Look for words like 'should,' 'must,' 'ought to,' 'is wrong,' 'is essential' — these signal argument. ANALYZE vs. COUNTER: an analytical passage examines something without necessarily trying to change anyone's mind; a counter passage specifically sets up an existing view and challenges it. Watch for 'contrary to popular belief,' 'this assumption is wrong,' 'the conventional view overlooks.'

For questions about the PURPOSE OF A SPECIFIC SENTENCE or PARAGRAPH within the passage, you must identify the sentence's ROLE IN THE ARGUMENT or narrative — not just what it says. Ask: 'Why is this sentence here? What does it do for the passage?' Common sentence-level purposes: introduces the topic, provides background context, gives supporting evidence, acknowledges a counterargument, transitions between ideas, or states the conclusion. The POSITION of the sentence in the passage (opening, middle, end) is a reliable clue about its purpose.
keys: Inform: presents facts neutrally, no clear position taken
Argue: takes a position, uses 'should/must/ought/is wrong'
Analyze: examines strengths AND weaknesses without necessarily advocating
Counter: sets up an existing view THEN challenges it directly
Describe: creates vivid detail, sensory language, often literary
Sentence purpose: ask WHY the sentence is there, not just WHAT it says
Position clue: opening sentence often introduces; final sentence often concludes

examples.t: Example 1 — Overall Purpose: Inform vs. Argue
examples.q:
Passage: 'The human gut contains approximately 38 trillion bacteria — nearly equal to the number of human cells in the body. These microorganisms, collectively called the gut microbiome, play critical roles in digestion, immune regulation, and the synthesis of certain vitamins. Recent research has also linked microbiome composition to mental health, with disruptions associated with increased rates of depression and anxiety.'

Which choice best describes the overall purpose of this text?
opts: To argue that doctors should prescribe probiotics for patients with depression
To explain the composition and significance of the gut microbiome
To counter the common belief that bacteria are harmful to human health
To describe the experience of living with a disrupted gut microbiome
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) To explain the composition and significance of the gut microbiome

The passage presents factual information about the gut microbiome: what it contains, what it does, and what research shows. It does not take a position ('should' or 'must'), does not counter a specific argument, and does not describe a personal experience. B is correct — the purpose is INFORMATIVE/EXPLANATORY. A is wrong (no recommendation about probiotics). C is wrong (no specific belief is being countered). D is wrong (no personal description).

examples.t: Example 2 — Overall Purpose: Counter vs. Analyze
examples.q:
Passage: 'Popular accounts of the Middle Ages routinely depict it as a period of intellectual stagnation — a 'Dark Age' between the brilliance of classical antiquity and the Renaissance. This characterization is deeply misleading. Medieval scholars translated, preserved, and extended classical knowledge. Institutions like the University of Bologna (founded 1088) and the University of Paris represent genuine intellectual centers that directly enabled Renaissance humanism. Dismissing the medieval period as intellectually barren is not only inaccurate but reflects a Renaissance-era propaganda that later historians have too uncritically inherited.'

Which choice best describes the overall purpose of this text?
opts: To analyze the major intellectual achievements of the medieval period
To persuade readers to study medieval history more seriously
To counter the characterization of the Middle Ages as intellectually stagnant
To describe the founding of medieval universities like Bologna and Paris
examples.a:
Correct answer: C) To counter the characterization of the Middle Ages as intellectually stagnant

The passage SPECIFICALLY sets up a commonly held view ('Dark Age' between antiquity and Renaissance) and then CHALLENGES IT ('This characterization is deeply misleading'). It provides evidence against this view and ends by attributing the misconception to Renaissance propaganda. C is correct — this is a COUNTER purpose. A is wrong (the passage doesn't systematically analyze medieval achievements; it refutes a specific claim). B is wrong (no explicit recommendation to study medieval history). D is wrong (universities are mentioned as evidence, not the focus).

examples.t: Example 3 — Purpose of a Specific Sentence
examples.q:
Passage: 'Many parents choose to enroll their children in after-school coding programs, believing this will prepare them for the technology-driven economy. [Sentence X: In 2023 alone, the US technology sector laid off over 260,000 workers.] This statistic suggests that the assumption of stable, growing tech employment underlying these enrollment decisions may be more fragile than parents recognize.'

Which choice best describes the function of Sentence X in the passage?
opts: To argue that parents should not enroll their children in coding programs
To provide evidence that complicates the assumption that technology careers offer stable employment
To counter the claim that the technology sector is an important part of the economy
To introduce the topic of the passage by establishing its economic context
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) To provide evidence that complicates the assumption that technology careers offer stable employment

Sentence X provides a SPECIFIC STATISTIC (260,000 layoffs) that is then explicitly interpreted by the next sentence as evidence that 'stable, growing tech employment' may be 'more fragile.' The statistic's purpose is to provide concrete evidence supporting the argument that parental assumptions about tech employment may be unreliable. B is correct. A is wrong — the passage questions assumptions, but Sentence X itself doesn't argue 'don't enroll.' C is wrong — the passage doesn't dispute tech's importance to the economy. D is wrong — the passage has already introduced its topic before Sentence X.

examples.q:
Passage: 'For decades, conservation policy in Africa was dominated by the 'fortress conservation' model, which established protected areas from which local communities were excluded. This approach was predicated on the assumption that human presence is inherently incompatible with wildlife preservation. Ethnographic and ecological research has since undermined this assumption: communities living alongside wildlife for generations have developed sophisticated management practices that maintain biodiversity, and exclusion has often led to resentment and poaching that undermines conservation goals.'

Which choice best describes the overall purpose of this text?
opts: To describe the history of wildlife conservation in Africa
To argue that the fortress conservation model should be immediately abolished
To challenge the assumption underlying fortress conservation by presenting contrary evidence
To analyze the strengths and weaknesses of multiple conservation approaches
examples.a:
Correct answer: C) To challenge the assumption underlying fortress conservation by presenting contrary evidence

The passage sets up the fortress conservation model and its underlying assumption ('human presence is inherently incompatible with wildlife'), then presents research that 'has since undermined this assumption.' The explicit structure — assumption presented, then challenged with evidence — makes this a COUNTER passage. C is correct. A is wrong (it's not a historical narrative; it's an argument). B is wrong (the passage questions the assumption but doesn't call for 'immediate abolition'). D is wrong (the passage critiques one approach, not multiple approaches comparatively).

examples.t: Example 5 — Purpose When Passage Ends with a Recommendation
examples.q:
Passage: 'Current environmental regulations in the United States require companies to disclose certain pollutants in public databases. However, these databases use different formats, are hosted on separate agency websites, and require technical expertise to interpret. Environmental scientists and legal scholars have consistently found that this fragmentation prevents both regulators and the public from identifying patterns of violation. Congress should establish a unified, publicly accessible environmental data portal that allows non-experts to search, visualize, and compare pollution data across regions and time periods.'

Which choice best describes the overall purpose of this text?
opts: To describe the current state of environmental data disclosure in the United States
To analyze the structural challenges facing environmental regulatory agencies
To argue for a specific policy reform to improve public access to environmental data
To counter the claim that environmental regulations are ineffective
examples.a:
Correct answer: C) To argue for a specific policy reform to improve public access to environmental data

The passage ends with an explicit recommendation: 'Congress SHOULD establish a unified...portal.' The word 'should' signals an ARGUMENT/PERSUASION purpose. The passage identifies a problem (fragmented databases) and advocates for a specific solution. C is correct. A is partially true (the current state is described) but only as background for the argument. B is partially true but 'analyze' misses the advocacy element — the author isn't just examining the problem but calling for action. D is wrong — the author doesn't counter a claim that regulations are ineffective; the author accepts the value of regulations and wants them improved.

sessions.title: Author's Perspective & Tone
theory: Perspective and tone questions ask about the AUTHOR'S ATTITUDE toward the subject. The question stems are: 'The author's attitude toward X can best be described as...' or 'Which choice best describes the author's perspective on Y?' Unlike purpose questions (which ask WHAT the author is doing), perspective questions ask HOW the author FEELS about the topic. The range of possible tones includes: critical, skeptical, alarmed, cautious, neutral/objective, celebratory, admiring, nostalgic, ironic, satirical, reluctantly accepting, cautiously optimistic.

The key strategy is to find EVALUATIVE LANGUAGE — adjectives, adverbs, and verbs that signal the author's feelings. 'Unfortunately,' 'remarkably,' 'troublingly,' 'merely,' 'only,' 'despite,' 'yet' — these small words carry tonal weight. Also look for WHAT THE AUTHOR CHOOSES TO EMPHASIZE: if an author describes both positive and negative aspects of something but devotes more space and stronger language to the negatives, the overall tone is critical. If the author acknowledges flaws but concludes with praise, the tone is measured admiration.

Common traps in tone questions: (1) CONFUSING TOPIC TONE with AUTHOR'S TONE — a passage about a tragic event can be written in a clinical, detached tone. The author's attitude is not necessarily emotional just because the topic is emotional. (2) TOO EXTREME vs. TOO MILD — if the author expresses concern, 'alarmed' may be too strong and 'interested' too mild. Look for the precision of fit. (3) SINGLE-SENTENCE BIAS — don't identify the tone from one sentence. Read the complete passage before committing. (4) CONFUSING REPORTED ATTITUDE with AUTHOR'S ATTITUDE — if the author says 'critics argue X is wrong,' the CRITICS' view is negative, but the author may be neutral or even supportive of X.
keys: Evaluative language: 'unfortunately,' 'remarkably,' 'merely,' 'troublingly,' 'despite'
Emphasis = attitude: more space + stronger words on X = author values/criticizes X
Tone precision: 'concerned' vs. 'alarmed' vs. 'distressed' — choose the best fit
Reported attitude ≠ author's attitude: critics say X is wrong ≠ author says X is wrong
Conclusion matters: how does the passage END? That often reveals final attitude
Neutral: facts presented without evaluative language, no clear position
Ironic: says one thing but means another, often via understatement or paradox

examples.t: Example 1 — Identifying Tone from Evaluative Language
examples.q:
Passage: 'The speed at which artificial intelligence systems are being deployed across critical sectors — healthcare, criminal justice, financial lending — has dramatically outpaced the development of oversight frameworks. Regulators, themselves often lacking technical expertise, are attempting to govern technologies they do not fully understand, while the companies deploying these systems have minimal incentives to slow their own expansion. The result has been a troubling series of documented failures: biased medical diagnostic tools, racially skewed criminal sentencing algorithms, and discriminatory lending models deployed to millions of users before their flaws were identified.'

The author's attitude toward the current deployment of AI systems can best be described as
opts: Cautiously optimistic about AI's long-term potential
Deeply concerned about the gap between deployment speed and adequate oversight
Neutral and objective in presenting both benefits and risks of AI
Nostalgic for a time before AI systems were used in critical decisions
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) Deeply concerned about the gap between deployment speed and adequate oversight

The evaluative language signals deep concern: 'dramatically outpaced,' 'attempting to govern technologies they do not fully understand,' 'minimal incentives to slow their own expansion,' and especially 'troubling series of documented failures.' The author presents NO positive aspects of AI deployment in this passage — only failures and oversight gaps. B is correct. A is wrong (no optimism is expressed). C is wrong (the author is not neutral — the language is strongly critical). D is wrong (no nostalgic longing for a pre-AI time is expressed).

examples.t: Example 2 — Nuanced Tone: Measured vs. Enthusiastic
examples.q:
Passage: 'Gene therapy — the technique of correcting defective genes to treat disease — has made remarkable strides in recent years. Several previously untreatable genetic conditions now have approved therapies, and clinical trials for dozens more are underway. Yet the field remains young, the cost of treatments prohibitively expensive for most patients globally, and the long-term durability of corrections in many conditions is still being established. The promise of gene therapy is genuine, but the distance between current capabilities and the transformative medicine its advocates envision remains considerable.'

The author's perspective on gene therapy can best be described as
opts: Enthusiastically supportive of gene therapy's achievements
Skeptical that gene therapy will ever achieve its promise
Cautiously optimistic, acknowledging both genuine achievements and significant remaining limitations
Neutral and detached, presenting information without evaluation
examples.a:
Correct answer: C) Cautiously optimistic, acknowledging both genuine achievements and significant remaining limitations

The passage acknowledges genuine achievements ('remarkable strides,' 'previously untreatable conditions now have approved therapies') while explicitly noting limitations ('cost prohibitively expensive,' 'long-term durability still being established,' 'distance... remains considerable'). The structure — achievements then limitations, ending with a note of remaining challenge — produces CAUTIOUS OPTIMISM. C is correct. A is wrong (the author's final note is about the 'considerable distance' remaining — not pure enthusiasm). B is wrong (the author does say the promise is 'genuine,' not that it will never be achieved). D is wrong (the language 'remarkable strides,' 'genuine promise' is evaluative, not neutral).

examples.t: Example 3 — Reported Attitude vs. Author's Attitude
examples.q:
Passage: 'Tech industry executives frequently describe their platforms as neutral conduits for information, arguing that they merely provide infrastructure for human communication and bear no more responsibility for their content than a telephone company bears for conversations on its lines. Legal scholars and regulators, however, increasingly argue that this analogy is false: unlike telephone companies, platforms actively curate, recommend, and algorithmically amplify content, shaping what users see in ways that traditional common carrier models were never designed to address.'

The author's own attitude toward the tech industry's 'neutral conduit' claim is best described as
opts: Supportive of the tech industry's position that platforms should not be regulated
Skeptical of the claim, as shown by the author's framing and the final contrast
Neutral, presenting both positions without indicating a preference
Alarmed that tech platforms are actively censoring communication
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) Skeptical of the claim, as shown by the author's framing and the final contrast

While the passage presents both views, the author's framing reveals their attitude. The executives' position is described as their own claim ('describe,' 'arguing'). The legal scholars' counterargument is introduced as 'however,' and the refutation is specific: 'this analogy is false' and 'platforms ACTIVELY curate' — the word 'actively' contrasted with the 'neutral conduit' claim shows the author sides with the critics. B is correct. A is wrong (the author doesn't support the industry position). C is wrong (the framing is not neutral — 'this analogy is false' is a strong evaluative statement). D is wrong (the passage is about algorithmic amplification/curation, not censorship).

examples.q:
Passage: 'The discovery that RNA could catalyze biochemical reactions — once thought to be the exclusive province of proteins — opened up entirely new research directions in molecular biology. The 'RNA world' hypothesis that followed offered an elegant potential solution to the chicken-and-egg problem of life's origins: which came first, the DNA that stores genetic information or the proteins that act on that information? RNA could, in principle, do both. The hypothesis remains controversial, with competing models and unresolved questions, but it has inspired decades of productive experimental work and fundamentally changed how scientists think about the origins of life.'

The author's attitude toward the RNA world hypothesis can best be described as
opts: Fully convinced that the RNA world hypothesis correctly explains life's origins
Critical of the hypothesis for remaining unresolved after decades of research
Appreciative of the hypothesis's intellectual contribution despite its unresolved status
Alarmed that scientists have not yet resolved the question of life's origins
examples.a:
Correct answer: C) Appreciative of the hypothesis's intellectual contribution despite its unresolved status

The author uses positive evaluative language: 'elegant potential solution,' 'inspired decades of productive experimental work,' 'fundamentally changed how scientists think.' Simultaneously, the author acknowledges that it 'remains controversial, with competing models and unresolved questions.' This combination — genuine appreciation for a hypothesis's intellectual contribution + honest acknowledgment of its limitations — is APPRECIATIVE/ADMIRING DESPITE LIMITATIONS. C is the most precise. A is wrong ('remains controversial' shows the author doesn't claim full conviction). B is wrong (the author does not criticize it for being unresolved — the decades of inspired work are presented positively). D is wrong (no alarm is expressed about unresolved questions).

examples.t: Example 5 — Recognizing Irony and Subtle Critique
examples.q:
Passage: 'The consulting firm's 400-page report on improving organizational communication at the company arrived six months late, was distributed only to senior executives who had already left the organization, and concluded — after extensive interviews, surveys, and data collection — that the primary obstacle to effective communication was that employees felt their concerns were not heard by senior management. The report recommended forming a working group to study the issue further.'

The author's attitude toward the consulting report can best be described as
opts: Admiring of the thoroughness and rigor of the consulting process
Ironically critical, using the report's own outcomes to expose its absurdity
Alarmed by the specific findings about employee concerns
Neutral and objective in describing what happened
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) Ironically critical, using the report's own outcomes to expose its absurdity

The author uses IRONY to critique the report: a 400-page report ON COMMUNICATION arrived late, went to people who had left, identified as its key finding that 'employees felt their concerns were not heard' (a self-referentially ironic finding), and recommended forming ANOTHER working group. The accumulation of absurdities — without the author ever directly saying 'this was useless' — creates sharp ironic critique. B is correct. A is wrong (no admiration is expressed — the details mock the process). C is wrong (the specific finding about employees is presented as part of the irony, not as something alarming). D is wrong (the selection of these specific absurd details is not neutral — the author is clearly critiquing).

sessions.title: Paired Passages — Understanding the Relationship
theory: Cross-text questions present TWO SHORT PASSAGES by different authors and ask about the relationship between them. The Digital SAT includes several paired passage sets per test. The most important first step: before answering any question, identify the RELATIONSHIP between the two texts. The four main relationships are: (1) AGREEMENT — both authors share the same position; (2) DISAGREEMENT/CONTRAST — the authors take opposing views on the same topic; (3) COMPLEMENTARY — the texts address different aspects of the same topic without directly contradicting each other; (4) EXTENSION — Text 2 builds on, develops, or applies what Text 1 establishes.

The most common cross-text question type asks: 'How would the author of Text 1 most likely respond to the argument in Text 2?' or 'Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree that...' For these questions, you must first identify each author's POSITION and then determine whether they would AGREE, DISAGREE, or have MIXED views. The trap: texts on the same topic can share vocabulary and examples while taking very different positions. Always identify the central CLAIM of each text before comparing them.

For AGREEMENT questions: find a statement that BOTH authors would endorse — not something one says explicitly and the other might possibly support, but something both clearly imply or argue. For DISAGREEMENT questions: find the exact point of divergence — on WHAT SPECIFIC ISSUE do the authors disagree? Two authors can agree on the facts but disagree on interpretation; agree on the problem but disagree on the solution; or disagree on fundamental assumptions.
keys: Step 1: Identify each author's central CLAIM before comparing
Step 2: Map the relationship (agree / disagree / complement / extend)
Agreement: both clearly support — not just 'might possibly support'
Disagreement: find the EXACT point of divergence, not just different topics
How would Author 1 respond? = find the overlap/gap between their positions
Trap: same topic + same vocabulary ≠ same position
Trap: authors can agree on facts but disagree on interpretation or implications

examples.q:
Text 1: 'Social media platforms should be regulated like public utilities because they have become essential infrastructure for public discourse. Just as telephone companies cannot discriminate in providing service, social media companies should be required to host all legal speech without algorithmic discrimination.'

Text 2: 'Treating social media platforms as public utilities misunderstands their nature. Unlike telephone networks, which passively transmit communication, social media platforms actively curate and amplify content. This editorial function is itself constitutionally protected expression — requiring platforms to host all speech regardless of content would effectively compel speech, which the First Amendment prohibits.'

Based on these texts, the authors would most likely disagree about which of the following?
opts: Whether social media has become an important part of public life
Whether social media platforms actively curate the content they display
Whether the public utility model is appropriate for regulating social media platforms
Whether telephone companies are regulated in the United States
examples.a:
Correct answer: C) Whether the public utility model is appropriate for regulating social media platforms

Text 1 ARGUES FOR the public utility model for social media. Text 2 ARGUES AGAINST it, specifically because platforms curate content (unlike passive telephone networks). Their disagreement is directly about whether the public utility regulatory model is appropriate for social media. C is correct. A is not a point of disagreement (both imply social media matters). B is actually a point of AGREEMENT (Text 2 explicitly says platforms 'actively curate,' while Text 1 implies editorial function by saying 'algorithmic discrimination'). D is not discussed as a point of disagreement.

examples.t: Example 2 — What Would Author 1 Say About Text 2?
examples.q:
Text 1: 'Standardized tests like the SAT were originally designed to identify talented students from non-elite backgrounds who lacked access to prestigious preparation. In practice, however, test scores correlate strongly with family income, primarily because wealthier families can afford test preparation courses, tutors, and multiple retakes. The test has become a mechanism for reproducing the privilege it was designed to disrupt.'

Text 2: 'Research consistently shows that SAT scores, when combined with high school GPA, predict college performance better than either measure alone. The test provides colleges with a standardized metric that supplements the varying standards of thousands of high schools nationwide. Eliminating the SAT from admissions without an equally valid alternative would reduce predictive accuracy.'

Based on Text 1, how would its author most likely respond to the argument in Text 2?
opts: By agreeing that the SAT's predictive validity justifies its continued use in admissions
By arguing that even if the SAT predicts college performance, this predictive validity does not address the concern that it reproduces economic inequality in admissions
By suggesting that high school GPA is a more reliable predictor than the SAT
By conceding that no alternative to standardized testing currently exists
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) By arguing that even if the SAT predicts college performance, this predictive validity does not address the concern that it reproduces economic inequality in admissions

Text 1's argument is specifically about the SAT reproducing economic inequality — that wealthy families can game the test. Text 2 argues the SAT predicts college performance. The Author of Text 1 would most likely say: 'Even if the SAT predicts performance, this doesn't address my concern about inequality.' B captures this response perfectly. A is wrong (Text 1 is clearly critical of the SAT). C is wrong (Text 1 doesn't mention GPA). D is wrong (Text 1 doesn't discuss alternatives).

examples.q:
Text 1: 'The global decline in insect populations poses an existential threat to agricultural systems. Insects pollinate approximately 75% of flowering crops; without them, yields would collapse. The primary drivers — pesticide use, habitat loss, and climate change — are all human-caused and could be addressed through policy reform.'

Text 2: 'While much attention has focused on iconic endangered species like polar bears and tigers, the quieter collapse of insect biodiversity may ultimately prove more consequential for human welfare. Insects sit at the base of most terrestrial food chains. Their decline cascades upward, affecting birds, mammals, and ultimately the agricultural systems that feed eight billion people.'

Based on both texts, what would both authors most likely agree on?
opts: That polar bears and tigers receive too much attention relative to insects
That pesticide use is the primary cause of insect population decline
That the decline of insect populations poses a serious threat to human food systems
That policy reform is the most effective solution to insect population collapse
examples.a:
Correct answer: C) That the decline of insect populations poses a serious threat to human food systems

Both texts explicitly connect insect decline to threats to human food/agricultural systems: Text 1 says 'yields would collapse'; Text 2 says the collapse 'cascades upward' to 'agricultural systems that feed eight billion people.' C is correct. A is only from Text 2 and is not in Text 1. B is only from Text 1 (Text 2 doesn't identify pesticides specifically). D is only from Text 1 (Text 2 makes no policy claim).

examples.q:
Text 1: 'Research on expert performance consistently challenges the intuition that talent is innate. Studies of musicians, chess players, and athletes show that practice hours — specifically deliberate, goal-directed practice — predict performance far better than any measured trait present at birth. The 10,000-hour figure, while an oversimplification, captures something real: expertise takes sustained effort.'

Text 2: 'The 'deliberate practice explains everything' model now faces significant pushback. Subsequent meta-analyses of the original studies found that deliberate practice explains approximately 26% of the variance in expert performance in games, 21% in music, and only 18% in sports. Something else — likely including domain-specific aptitude, early developmental exposure, and motivational factors — accounts for the majority of variance.'

Which choice best describes the relationship between the two texts?
opts: Text 2 fully confirms and extends the argument made in Text 1
Text 2 challenges the strength of the central claim in Text 1 by presenting subsequent research that shows deliberate practice is less explanatory than originally claimed
The two texts address completely different topics and cannot be directly compared
Text 2 presents the same argument as Text 1 but focuses specifically on sports performance
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) Text 2 challenges the strength of the central claim in Text 1 by presenting subsequent research that shows deliberate practice is less explanatory than originally claimed

Text 1 argues deliberate practice is the primary driver of expert performance. Text 2 presents later research showing practice explains only 18-26% of variance — CHALLENGING the 'practice explains everything' model. B correctly describes Text 2 as challenging Text 1's claim using subsequent research. A is wrong (Text 2 challenges, not confirms). C is wrong (both address expert performance). D is wrong (they present different arguments).

examples.q:
Text 1: 'The Roman Empire's engineering achievements — roads, aqueducts, sewage systems — enabled the remarkable administrative efficiency that sustained a polity spanning three continents. Without reliable infrastructure, the communication and supply chains that held the empire together could not have functioned.'

Text 2: 'Roman military dominance rested not only on tactical innovation but on institutional design: the professional legionary system created disciplined, standardized fighting forces that could be deployed reliably across diverse terrain. The empire conquered and held territory through organizational excellence as much as battlefield prowess.'

Which choice best describes the relationship between the two texts?
opts: The texts disagree about whether Roman engineering or military power was more important
Text 2 directly counters the central claim in Text 1
The texts complement each other, both arguing that Roman success depended on systematic organization rather than any single genius or advantage
Text 1 provides the historical context for the argument Text 2 makes about Roman military tactics
examples.a:
Correct answer: C) The texts complement each other, both arguing that Roman success depended on systematic organization rather than any single genius or advantage

Both texts argue that Roman success came from SYSTEMATIC ORGANIZATION: Text 1 attributes it to engineering/infrastructure; Text 2 attributes it to institutional military design. Neither contradicts the other — they address different domains (civil vs. military) but share a common thesis about systematic excellence. C is correct. A is wrong (neither text makes a comparative 'more important' claim). B is wrong (Text 2 doesn't counter Text 1 — they address different aspects). D is wrong (Text 1 doesn't provide context for Text 2's argument).

sessions.title: Answering Cross-Text Questions Precisely
theory: For 'How would Author 1 respond to Text 2?' questions, follow a strict three-step process: (1) IDENTIFY Author 1's central position precisely — not just the topic, but the specific claim. (2) IDENTIFY what Text 2 actually argues — again, the specific claim, not just the topic. (3) Apply Author 1's position to Text 2's argument: would Author 1 agree, partially agree, or disagree, and on what specific grounds? The answer must be grounded in BOTH texts — not in general knowledge about the topic.

Common traps in 'How would Author 1 respond?' questions: (1) The answer accurately describes Author 1's position but doesn't actually respond to Text 2's specific argument. (2) The answer correctly identifies a disagreement but mischaracterizes the REASON for it. (3) The answer has Author 1 agreeing with an element of Text 2 that Author 1 never actually addresses. (4) The answer describes what AUTHOR 2 would say, not Author 1. Always re-read the question to confirm which author you're being asked about.

For 'Both authors would agree that...' questions: eliminate answers that are from only ONE author. The correct answer must be something that BOTH texts independently support — not just something consistent with one and not contradicted by the other. 'Not contradicted by' is weaker than 'supported by.' The correct answer should be something you could point to evidence for in BOTH texts.
keys: Step 1: Author 1's exact claim | Step 2: Text 2's exact claim | Step 3: Match/clash
Trap: answer describes Author 1's position but doesn't respond to Text 2's SPECIFIC argument
Trap: confuses which author you're asked about (re-read the question!)
Agreement: find evidence in BOTH texts — not just 'not contradicted by one'
Partial agreement: one author endorses the facts but disputes the interpretation
Point the specific line in each text that supports your answer choice
Wrong: Author 1 agrees with something Text 2 says that Author 1 never addresses

examples.q:
Text 1: 'The growing use of facial recognition technology by law enforcement agencies presents a serious civil liberties threat. Current systems misidentify Black individuals at rates up to 34% higher than white individuals, creating systematic racial bias in policing. Until this accuracy gap is closed, facial recognition should not be used in any law enforcement context.'

Text 2: 'Facial recognition technology, properly deployed, can significantly improve law enforcement efficiency and accuracy. When used to generate investigative leads — not as standalone proof of identity — and when combined with human review, it can help solve serious crimes that would otherwise go unpunished. The question is not whether to use the technology but how to regulate its use appropriately.'

Based on Text 1, how would its author most likely respond to the argument in Text 2?
opts: By agreeing that facial recognition is useful for generating investigative leads
By arguing that even properly regulated use of facial recognition cannot address the underlying accuracy disparity that disproportionately harms Black individuals
By suggesting that human review is sufficient to overcome the technology's accuracy problems
By conceding that facial recognition has legitimate uses but calling for stronger privacy regulations
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) By arguing that even properly regulated use of facial recognition cannot address the underlying accuracy disparity that disproportionately harms Black individuals

Text 1's specific concern is the RACIAL ACCURACY GAP — misidentification of Black individuals at 34% higher rates. Text 2 argues for regulated, human-reviewed use. Author of Text 1 would say: even regulated use doesn't fix the accuracy disparity that creates racial bias. B directly applies Text 1's specific concern (accuracy gap + racial harm) to Text 2's proposal. A is wrong (Text 1 calls for no law enforcement use at all). C is wrong (Text 1 doesn't accept human review as a sufficient fix). D is wrong (Text 1 doesn't endorse 'legitimate uses with regulation').

examples.q:
Text 1: 'Universal basic income would provide workers with genuine bargaining power: knowing they have an income floor, they could leave exploitative employment rather than endure it. This freedom from economic coercion would improve wages and conditions across the economy through market competition rather than regulation.'

Text 2: 'A universal basic income could provide economic security for individuals facing job displacement from automation. However, the amount required to replace existing welfare programs and provide a genuine living floor would cost trillions annually — a fiscal reality that makes truly universal and adequate UBI politically and economically impractical in most nations in the near term.'

Based on both texts, what would both authors most likely agree on?
opts: That UBI would be economically sustainable with appropriate fiscal planning
That UBI could provide beneficial economic security for individuals in certain circumstances
That UBI should replace existing welfare programs
That automation is the primary justification for implementing a UBI
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) That UBI could provide beneficial economic security for individuals in certain circumstances

Text 1 argues UBI provides workers economic security to leave exploitative employment. Text 2 says UBI 'could provide economic security for individuals facing job displacement.' Both acknowledge UBI's potential to provide beneficial economic security. B is the shared point. A is wrong (only Text 1 implies sustainability; Text 2 argues it's fiscally impractical). C is wrong (only Text 2 mentions replacing welfare programs — and questions it). D is wrong (only Text 2 mentions automation; Text 1 focuses on labor bargaining power).

examples.q:
Text 1: 'Ancient Greek democracy was profoundly limited by modern standards: it excluded women, enslaved people, and non-citizens — the majority of the resident population. To call Athenian democracy a 'democracy' without qualification is to accept the Greeks' own self-description uncritically.'

Text 2: 'Whatever its exclusions, Athenian democracy represented a genuine conceptual breakthrough: the idea that a political community could be self-governing, that citizens had both the right and the obligation to participate directly in decisions affecting them. The exclusions were real but were features of their time, not of the democratic concept itself.'

Based on Text 2, how would its author most likely respond to the argument in Text 1?
opts: By agreeing that Athenian democracy should not be called a democracy at all
By conceding that the exclusions were severe while arguing that they don't negate the genuine conceptual innovation of democratic self-governance
By arguing that women and enslaved people had more political influence than Text 1 acknowledges
By suggesting that modern democracy has also failed to include all people equally
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) By conceding that the exclusions were severe while arguing that they don't negate the genuine conceptual innovation of democratic self-governance

Text 2 explicitly acknowledges 'the exclusions were real' (conceding Text 1's point) but argues they were 'features of their time, not of the democratic concept itself' — meaning the concept of democratic self-governance is still valuable. B precisely captures this 'concede the facts, defend the concept' response. A is wrong (Text 2 defends calling it democracy). C is wrong (Text 2 doesn't make this argument). D is wrong (Text 2 doesn't mention modern democracy).

sessions.title: Rhetorical Effectiveness — Adding, Deleting & Placement
theory: Some of the SAT's hardest questions ask whether a sentence SHOULD BE ADDED or DELETED, or WHERE a sentence should be placed. For ADDING: a sentence should be added only if it directly supports the paragraph's central purpose — not if it's merely related to the general topic. Ask: does this sentence provide specific support for the argument being made, or does it introduce a tangential idea? Adding tangential information, no matter how interesting, weakens a focused paragraph.

For DELETING: a sentence should be deleted if it (a) contradicts the paragraph's point, (b) introduces information already covered elsewhere, (c) digresses from the focus, or (d) is too general to serve as evidence. The question usually asks 'Should this sentence be kept or deleted? Why?' The correct answer identifies the SPECIFIC FUNCTION the sentence serves (or fails to serve) in its paragraph. Vague answers like 'it adds detail' are usually wrong — the detail must be the RIGHT KIND.

For PLACEMENT: a sentence fits best where (a) the content logically follows what precedes it, (b) the transition words connect to the surrounding context, and (c) it leads naturally into what follows. Look for CONTENT BRIDGES — the new sentence's subject or key terms should connect to terms introduced just before the target location. Also check whether the sentence's transition signals (however, furthermore, for example) match the logical relationship needed at that point.
keys: Add only if: directly supports the paragraph's specific argument
Delete if: tangential, contradicts, repeats, or too general to serve as evidence
Placement: where content bridges are strongest (key terms connect before and after)
Transition test: does 'however/furthermore/for example' fit the relationship needed?
Wrong add answer: 'it provides interesting information' — must be RELEVANT information
Correct delete reason: 'it shifts focus from X to Y' — specific, not vague
Always consider the PARAGRAPH'S PURPOSE before evaluating a sentence

examples.t: Example 1 — Should This Sentence Be Added?
examples.q:
Paragraph: 'Urban heat islands occur when cities trap heat due to pavement, buildings, and reduced vegetation. Studies show they can raise urban temperatures by 2-5°C above surrounding rural areas. [Proposed addition: The history of city planning dates back to ancient Mesopotamia.] This temperature difference increases energy demand for cooling and worsens air quality.'

Should the proposed sentence be added?
opts: Yes — it provides useful background context about urban development
Yes — it explains why cities have become more vulnerable to heat islands
No — it shifts focus from the specific problem being discussed (heat islands) to a broadly related but irrelevant historical topic
No — it contradicts the claim that heat islands are caused by modern development
examples.a:
Correct answer: C) No — it shifts focus from the specific problem being discussed (heat islands) to a broadly related but irrelevant historical topic

The paragraph is specifically about urban heat islands, their causes, and effects. The history of ancient city planning does not support or advance this argument — it's merely topically adjacent to 'cities.' C correctly identifies the reason: it shifts focus to an irrelevant topic. A and B are wrong because relevance requires direct support, not just general connection.

examples.t: Example 2 — Where Should This Sentence Go?
examples.q:
Paragraph: '[1] Citizen science projects have expanded dramatically in the past decade. [2] Thousands of volunteers contribute observations to research on bird migration, water quality, and galaxy classification. [3] However, data quality concerns have limited their use in peer-reviewed research. [4] Some studies have found error rates significantly higher than in professionally collected data.'

Where should the following sentence be inserted: 'These accuracy concerns have prompted researchers to develop new verification protocols'?
opts: After sentence 1
After sentence 2
After sentence 3
After sentence 4
examples.a:
Correct answer: D) After sentence 4

The new sentence about 'accuracy concerns' and 'verification protocols' directly responds to 'error rates' mentioned in Sentence 4 — and logically transitions: error rates exist (S4) → researchers respond with verification (new sentence). After S4 is most logical. C (after S3) would place it before the specific error rate evidence.

examples.t: Example 3 — Should This Sentence Be Deleted?
examples.q:
Paragraph: 'The Amazon rainforest stores approximately 150-200 billion tons of carbon, making it critical to global climate stability. Deforestation releases this stored carbon and simultaneously eliminates the forest's future carbon absorption capacity. [Sentence X: The Amazon basin also contains the world's largest river by discharge volume.] Both effects compound over time, accelerating the pace of climate change.'

Should Sentence X be kept or deleted?
opts: Kept — it provides important geographical context for the Amazon's global significance
Kept — it explains why the Amazon river contributes to carbon storage
Deleted — it introduces a geographical fact that does not connect to the paragraph's focus on carbon and climate
Deleted — it contradicts the paragraph's claim about the Amazon's size
examples.a:
Correct answer: C) Deleted — it introduces a geographical fact that does not connect to the paragraph's focus on carbon and climate

The paragraph is specifically about carbon storage and climate change. The Amazon river's discharge volume is a geographical fact that doesn't connect to carbon, deforestation, or climate change. C correctly identifies the reason: it doesn't connect to the paragraph's focus. A is wrong — geographic significance doesn't serve the carbon/climate argument. B is wrong — the river discharge doesn't explain carbon storage.

examples.q:
Passage: 'Traditional economic models assume that consumers make rational decisions to maximize utility. [___], behavioral economics has demonstrated that humans consistently make predictable irrational choices — influenced by framing, loss aversion, and cognitive biases.'

Which transition best completes the text?
opts: Furthermore
Therefore
However
For example
examples.a:
Correct answer: C) However

The relationship is CONTRAST: traditional models say rational decisions; behavioral economics shows irrational choices. CONTRAST → However. C is correct. A (furthermore) adds; doesn't contrast. B (therefore) shows a result — but behavioral economics isn't a result of traditional models. D (for example) introduces an example.

examples.q:
Paragraph: 'The gig economy has created flexible employment for millions but also introduced new forms of economic precarity. Without benefits like health insurance, workers bear greater individual risk. Income volatility makes long-term financial planning difficult. [Proposed conclusion: These challenges suggest that existing labor regulations, designed for traditional employment relationships, may be inadequate for the gig economy.]

Should this concluding sentence be added?
opts: No — the paragraph already makes a conclusion about the gig economy
Yes — it explicitly connects the specific problems described to a broader policy implication, providing the paragraph a meaningful conclusion
No — it introduces new information about labor regulations that is outside the scope of the paragraph
Yes — any concluding sentence improves a paragraph's structure
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) Yes — it explicitly connects the specific problems described to a broader policy implication, providing the paragraph a meaningful conclusion

The paragraph describes specific problems (no benefits, income volatility) but leaves them without a 'so what.' The proposed sentence connects these specific observations to a broader, relevant implication — inadequacy of existing labor law. B correctly identifies this function. A is wrong — the paragraph has no current conclusion. C is wrong — connecting to labor regulations is directly relevant to the problems described. D is too generic.

sessions.title: Rhetorical Purpose & Word Choice at the 800 Level
theory: At the 750-800 level, the SAT tests subtle word choice distinctions within a rhetorical context. Words that are nearly synonymous may differ in CONNOTATION (positive, negative, neutral), REGISTER (formal, informal, technical), PRECISION (specific vs. vague), and IMPLICATION (what the word signals about the author's perspective). 'The policy FAILED' vs. 'The policy UNDERPERFORMED' vs. 'The policy DID NOT ACHIEVE ITS STATED GOALS' — each signals a different level of judgment and a different relationship between the author and the subject.

RHETORICAL PURPOSE questions ask: which word or phrase best accomplishes the writer's apparent purpose in this context? The answer depends on understanding: (1) the passage's overall tone (academic/neutral, critical, sympathetic, ironic), (2) the audience (general public, specialists, policymakers), and (3) the paragraph's specific argumentative purpose at this moment. A word appropriate for a personal essay may be wrong in an academic paper. A hedging word ('may suggest') may be wrong when the evidence is conclusive.

TRANSITIONS AS RHETORICAL SIGNALS: beyond grammar, transitions signal the logical structure of the argument. On the SAT, transitions are tested not only for grammatical correctness but for RHETORICAL FIT — does this transition accurately signal the logical relationship that exists between the two ideas? 'The evidence is weak; nevertheless, the conclusion is strong' vs. 'The evidence is weak; therefore, the conclusion is strong' — both are grammatically correct; only one is logically accurate. Always check the relationship.
keys: Word choice: consider connotation, register, precision, and implication
Stronger judgment words: failed, flawed, inadequate vs. underperformed, limited
Hedging language: may suggest, appears to, could indicate — for uncertain evidence
Definitive language: demonstrates, confirms, establishes — for strong evidence
Register: academic paper = formal; op-ed = more direct; technical audience = precise
Rhetorical purpose: what is this paragraph trying to DO at this moment?
Transition fit: does the transition accurately reflect the logical relationship?

examples.q:
Context: A scientific paper discussing a study with mixed results.

Text: 'The intervention [___] the expected outcomes in approximately half the test conditions.'

Which word best fits the formal, measured tone of a scientific report?
opts: failed to produce
did not achieve
bombed
fell disappointingly short of
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) did not achieve

In a scientific paper, language should be precise and emotionally neutral. B ('did not achieve') is the most formally neutral — it states the outcome without judgment. A ('failed') implies a more definitive negative judgment. C ('bombed') is informal slang. D ('fell disappointingly short') introduces emotional evaluation inappropriate for scientific reporting.

examples.q:
Context: A passage presenting preliminary research findings.

Text: 'The correlation between screen time and attention deficits [___] a causal relationship.'

Which phrase is most appropriate given that only a correlation (not causation) has been established?
opts: proves
establishes
does not indicate
may suggest
examples.a:
Correct answer: D) may suggest

A correlation study cannot prove causation. D ('may suggest') appropriately hedges — acknowledging the correlation without claiming causation. A ('proves') and B ('establishes') both overclaim for correlational data. C ('does not indicate') is too dismissive — the correlation does suggest something, just not causation.

examples.q:
Context: An op-ed arguing for criminal justice reform.

Text: 'The current system [___] those who are most economically disadvantaged, perpetuating cycles of poverty and incarceration.'

Which phrase best fits an op-ed's direct, persuasive register?
opts: may possibly disproportionately affect
disproportionately targets
could in some cases disadvantage
has been shown in some studies to negatively impact
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) disproportionately targets

An op-ed is argumentative and direct — it should state positions clearly, not hedge. B ('disproportionately targets') is strong, direct, and uses precise language ('disproportionately' is accurate; 'targets' suggests deliberate structural effect). A and C hedge unnecessarily. D is overly academic and passive for an op-ed.

examples.q:
Text: 'Historical data shows that economic growth often slows during periods of high inflation. The central bank raised interest rates last month.'

Which transition most accurately connects these sentences?
opts: Moreover, the central bank raised interest rates last month.
For example, the central bank raised interest rates last month.
In response to these inflationary pressures, the central bank raised interest rates last month.
Nevertheless, the central bank raised interest rates last month.
examples.a:
Correct answer: C) In response to these inflationary pressures, the central bank raised interest rates last month.

The relationship is CAUSE AND EFFECT or CONTEXT TO ACTION: inflation (established in S1) prompted the central bank to act. C ('In response to these inflationary pressures') directly connects the cause to the effect. A ('moreover') adds, doesn't connect cause/effect. B ('for example') makes the rate increase an example of slowing growth — illogical. D ('nevertheless') implies contrast — the bank acted despite the trend.

examples.t: Example 5 — Word Choice for Argument Strength
examples.q:
Context: A paragraph concluding an argument about the inadequacy of plastic bag bans.

Text: 'The evidence reviewed here [___] that single-use plastic bag bans, while symbolically significant, have not substantially reduced total plastic pollution.'

Which phrase best fits the conclusion of a well-supported argument?
opts: might possibly imply
raises questions about whether
suggests
demonstrates
examples.a:
Correct answer: D) demonstrates

For a conclusion that summarizes reviewed evidence, the language should be proportional to the strength of the evidence. D ('demonstrates') is appropriate for a conclusion where the evidence is presented as definitive. C ('suggests') is appropriate for preliminary or incomplete evidence. A and B are overly hedged for a paragraph presenting its conclusion. Given that the passage says 'evidence reviewed here,' D is appropriately confident.

sessions.title: Rhetorical Synthesis — What the Question Is Actually Asking
theory: Rhetorical Synthesis questions present a set of bulleted notes and ask you to combine the relevant information to accomplish a specific RHETORICAL GOAL. The question stem tells you exactly what goal the student is trying to achieve: 'The student wants to introduce the topic by presenting a surprising contrast,' or 'The student wants to provide evidence supporting the claim that...,' or 'The student wants to emphasize X while acknowledging Y.' Your job is to find the answer choice that accomplishes that SPECIFIC GOAL using information from the notes.

The most important skill: READ THE GOAL CAREFULLY before looking at the answer choices. The notes give you the raw material; the goal tells you what to BUILD from that material. A note might contain five facts, but the goal might only require one specific fact, presented in a specific way. Wrong answers often: (1) use correct information but fail to accomplish the stated goal; (2) accomplish a DIFFERENT goal than the one stated; (3) use information NOT in the notes; (4) combine information in a way that creates a DIFFERENT emphasis than the goal requires.

Common rhetorical goals on the SAT include: INTRODUCE with surprising or interesting detail; SUPPORT a specific claim with evidence from the notes; EMPHASIZE a contrast or comparison; ACKNOWLEDGE a limitation or counterpoint; CONCLUDE by connecting a specific detail to a broader point. For each goal type, you must identify which specific pieces of note information are RELEVANT to the goal and which answer choice BEST SERVES the goal. Often two answer choices use correct information, but only one accomplishes the specific goal stated.
keys: Step 1: Read the GOAL before reading the answer choices
Step 2: Identify which notes are RELEVANT to the goal
Step 3: Find the choice that accomplishes the goal (not just uses correct info)
Trap: uses correct information but serves a DIFFERENT goal
Trap: uses information NOT in the notes
Trap: two choices use correct info — only one achieves the SPECIFIC goal
Goal types: introduce, support, contrast, acknowledge, conclude, emphasize

examples.q:
Notes:
• Monarch butterflies migrate up to 3,000 miles annually
• Migration is guided by a sun compass and circadian clock
• Population has declined 80% in 30 years
• Main causes: milkweed habitat loss and climate change
• Some populations now overwinter in California, not just Mexico

The student wants to support the claim that monarch butterfly migration requires sophisticated navigation mechanisms.

Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes?
opts: Monarch butterflies migrate up to 3,000 miles annually, and their population has declined by 80% over the past 30 years.

Their migration is guided by a sun compass that uses the position of the sun in combination with an internal circadian clock to maintain directional orientation — a navigation system of remarkable complexity.
Because milkweed habitat loss and climate change have caused population decline, some monarchs now overwinter in California rather than Mexico.
Monarch butterflies travel up to 3,000 miles each year, making their journey one of the longest insect migrations in the world.
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) Their migration is guided by a sun compass that uses the position of the sun in combination with an internal circadian clock to maintain directional orientation — a navigation system of remarkable complexity.

The goal is to support the claim about SOPHISTICATED NAVIGATION MECHANISMS. B directly addresses this: it describes the sun compass + circadian clock system and explicitly calls it 'a navigation system of remarkable complexity' — supporting the 'sophisticated' claim. A uses the distance and population decline facts — neither supports the navigation claim. C describes habitat/climate causes and range shifts — not navigation. D uses distance only, not the navigation mechanism.

examples.t: Example 2 — Introducing with a Surprising Contrast
examples.q:
Notes:
• James Watson and Francis Crick won 1962 Nobel Prize for DNA structure
• Their discovery was based on X-ray diffraction data produced by Rosalind Franklin
• Franklin was not credited in their 1953 paper
• Franklin died in 1958, four years before the Nobel was awarded
• Nobel Prize cannot be awarded posthumously

The student wants to introduce the topic by highlighting an irony in the Nobel Prize story.

Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes?
opts: James Watson and Francis Crick won the Nobel Prize in 1962 for determining the structure of DNA, a discovery with profound implications for biology and medicine.
Rosalind Franklin produced the X-ray diffraction data that Watson and Crick relied upon to determine DNA's structure, yet she was not credited in their original 1953 paper.

The scientists whose X-ray data made possible the 1962 Nobel Prize-winning discovery of DNA's structure died four years before the award was given — and the Nobel Prize cannot be awarded posthumously, making recognition impossible regardless of committee decisions.
Rosalind Franklin worked at King's College London, while Watson and Crick worked at Cambridge.
examples.a:
Correct answer: C) The scientists whose X-ray data made possible the 1962 Nobel Prize-winning discovery of DNA's structure died four years before the award was given — and the Nobel Prize cannot be awarded posthumously, making recognition impossible regardless of committee decisions.

The goal is to highlight an IRONY in the Nobel Prize story. C presents the irony precisely: Franklin's data enabled the prize-winning discovery, but she died four years before the award — and the Nobel cannot be given posthumously, making the irony complete (she couldn't have won even if alive, because she died before the prize was awarded). A introduces Watson and Crick's Nobel without any irony. B presents the uncredited data problem but without the Nobel Prize irony specifically. D is a factual detail with no ironic contrast.

examples.q:
Notes:
• Average CEO pay at S&P 500 companies: $16.7 million in 2022
• Average worker pay at same companies: $55,000 in 2022
• CEO-to-worker pay ratio: ~300:1
• In 1965, the ratio was approximately 21:1
• Japan's CEO-to-worker ratio averages approximately 10:1

The student wants to emphasize how dramatically the CEO-to-worker pay gap has changed over time.

Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes?
opts: American CEOs earn approximately 300 times more than their average workers, and CEOs at comparable Japanese companies earn approximately 10 times more than their workers.
The CEO-to-worker pay ratio at major American companies has grown from approximately 21:1 in 1965 to approximately 300:1 in 2022, a more than fourteenfold increase over six decades.
Average CEO pay at S&P 500 companies was $16.7 million in 2022, while the average worker at the same companies earned $55,000.
The growing gap between executive and worker compensation reflects broader trends toward income inequality in the American economy.
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) The CEO-to-worker pay ratio at major American companies has grown from approximately 21:1 in 1965 to approximately 300:1 in 2022, a more than fourteenfold increase over six decades.

The goal is to emphasize how dramatically the gap has CHANGED OVER TIME. B uses the historical comparison (21:1 in 1965 → 300:1 in 2022) and explicitly quantifies the change ('more than fourteenfold increase over six decades') — directly serving the 'change over time' goal. A uses the US-Japan comparison (not the historical change). C presents current pay figures without any historical comparison. D is a vague general statement not from the notes.

examples.q:
Notes:
• Exercise has been shown to reduce symptoms of mild-to-moderate depression
• Meta-analysis of 41 studies showed exercise as effective as antidepressants for this group
• Most studies used self-reported outcomes (subjective)
