opts: Because the satellite lost communication. Mission control improvised a solution.
Because the satellite lost communication, mission control improvised a solution.
Because the satellite lost communication; mission control improvised a solution.
Because the satellite lost communication and mission control improvised a solution.
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) Because the satellite lost communication, mission control improvised a solution.

A has a fragment ('Because the satellite lost communication' alone) followed by a separate sentence. B correctly attaches the dependent clause to the main clause with a comma. C incorrectly uses a semicolon after a dependent clause. D creates a run-on with unclear structure.

examples.q: Which version is a complete sentence (not a fragment)?
opts: The professor, having spent thirty years studying migration patterns.
Having spent thirty years studying migration patterns, the professor published her definitive account.
Having spent thirty years studying migration patterns.
The professor spending thirty years studying migration patterns.
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) Having spent thirty years studying migration patterns, the professor published her definitive account.

B: 'Having spent thirty years...' is an introductory participial phrase, followed by 'the professor published her definitive account' (subject + complete verb). It is a complete sentence. A has no main verb after 'the professor.' C is only the participial phrase. D has no main verb.

examples.q:
A student writes: 'Climate change poses significant risks to coastal communities. Particularly those in low-lying areas vulnerable to storm surges and sea-level rise.'

The second sentence is a fragment. Which is the best fix?
opts: Climate change poses significant risks to coastal communities; particularly those in low-lying areas.
Climate change poses significant risks to coastal communities, particularly those in low-lying areas vulnerable to storm surges and sea-level rise.
Climate change poses significant risks. To coastal communities particularly those in low-lying areas.
Climate change poses significant risks to coastal communities. Those are in low-lying areas vulnerable.
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) Climate change poses significant risks to coastal communities, particularly those in low-lying areas vulnerable to storm surges and sea-level rise.

B attaches the fragment to the preceding sentence with a comma, creating one complete sentence. A uses a semicolon before a fragment. C creates two fragments. D changes meaning and is still awkward.

examples.q:
Text: 'The ancient temple [___] for over two thousand years before archaeologists uncovered it in 1987.'

Which choice makes this a complete sentence?
opts: standing hidden
which stood hidden
stood hidden
having stood hidden
examples.a:
Correct answer: C) stood hidden

C: 'stood hidden' — 'stood' is a complete past tense verb. Subject = 'The ancient temple,' verb = 'stood.' Complete sentence. A ('standing') = participial — no complete verb. B ('which stood') = relative clause — 'which' makes it dependent. D ('having stood') = participial — no complete verb.

sessions.title: Modifiers — Placement & Dangling Modifiers
theory: A MODIFIER is a word, phrase, or clause that describes something else. The SAT tests two modifier errors. (1) MISPLACED MODIFIER: the modifier is in the wrong position — too far from what it modifies, making the sentence ambiguous or illogical. 'She almost drove her children to school every day' (almost modifies drove — she nearly drove but didn't?) vs. 'She drove her children to almost every school' (correct placement). (2) DANGLING MODIFIER: the thing being modified is not in the sentence at all, or is not the subject of the main clause. 'Walking down the street, the trees were beautiful.' — the trees were not walking. Fix: 'Walking down the street, I noticed the trees were beautiful.'

IDENTIFYING DANGLING MODIFIERS: when a sentence opens with a participial phrase (-ing or -ed), the subject of the main clause MUST be the thing performing or experiencing the action in the phrase. Test: who is doing the -ing? That entity must be the subject immediately after the comma. 'Exhausted after the long hike, the tent was pitched' — the tent isn't exhausted. Correct: 'Exhausted after the long hike, the hikers pitched their tent.' The subject ('hikers') must immediately follow the introductory phrase.

ONLY, ALMOST, NEARLY, JUST, EVEN: these limiting modifiers must immediately precede the word they modify because their placement changes meaning. 'Only I told him the truth' (no one else told him). 'I only told him the truth' (I merely told him, did nothing else). 'I told only him the truth' (I told him and no one else). 'I told him only the truth' (I told the truth and nothing else). On the SAT, pay careful attention to where these words are placed in answer choices.
keys: Modifier must be ADJACENT to what it modifies
Dangling modifier: opening phrase must match the SUBJECT of the main clause
'Opening phrase, SUBJECT VERB' — subject must be performing the phrase's action
Only/almost/just/nearly: place immediately before the word they limit
Test dangling: ask 'WHO is [verb]-ing?' — that entity must be the subject
Misplaced: ambiguous | Dangling: illogical (impossible for subject to do the action)
Fix dangling: change subject OR restructure the phrase

examples.q:
Which version correctly fixes the dangling modifier?

A) Having reviewed the evidence, the verdict was announced by the jury.
B) Having reviewed the evidence, the jury announced its verdict.
C) The verdict, having reviewed the evidence, was announced.
D) The jury announced its verdict, having reviewed the evidence carefully.
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) B

'Having reviewed the evidence' — who reviewed the evidence? The jury. The subject immediately after the comma must be 'the jury.' B is correct. A has 'the verdict' as subject — the verdict didn't review evidence. C places the participial phrase as a nonrestrictive element (illogical). D reverses the order but works, though B is cleaner.

examples.q:
Which version correctly places the modifier 'only'?

Original: 'The study only found evidence of improvement in patients who exercised for at least 30 minutes.'

If the intended meaning is that improvement was found exclusively in patients who exercised (not in those who did not), which version is best?
opts: The study only found evidence of improvement in patients who exercised.
The study found evidence only of improvement in patients who exercised.
The study found evidence of improvement only in patients who exercised.
Only the study found evidence of improvement in patients who exercised.
examples.a:
Correct answer: C) The study found evidence of improvement only in patients who exercised.

'Only in patients who exercised' limits WHERE improvement was found. C places 'only' immediately before 'in patients who exercised,' correctly specifying that the improvement was exclusive to the exercising group. A places 'only' before 'found' (modifies the finding, not the location). B limits to improvement (vs. other effects). D implies no other studies found evidence.

examples.q: Which version correctly uses the opening participial phrase?
opts: Designed to withstand extreme weather, engineers tested the bridge for three years.
Designed to withstand extreme weather, the bridge was tested for three years.
Designed to withstand extreme weather, the bridge's testing took three years.
The bridge, designed to withstand extreme weather, engineers tested for three years.
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) Designed to withstand extreme weather, the bridge was tested for three years.

'Designed to withstand extreme weather' modifies the bridge (the bridge was designed). The subject after the comma must be 'the bridge.' B is correct. A makes 'engineers' the subject (engineers weren't designed for weather). C uses 'the bridge's testing' — a gerund as subject, not the bridge itself. D misplaces the phrase.

examples.q:
Original sentence: 'Researchers almost documented every species in the rainforest.'

If the intended meaning is that researchers documented nearly all (but not quite all) species, which revision is best?
opts: Researchers almost documented every species in the rainforest.
Researchers documented almost every species in the rainforest.
Almost researchers documented every species in the rainforest.
Researchers documented every species almost in the rainforest.
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) Researchers documented almost every species in the rainforest.

To convey that nearly all species were documented, 'almost' must modify 'every species.' B: 'documented almost every species' — 'almost' directly precedes 'every species.' A places 'almost' before 'documented' — meaning researchers came close to doing the documentation but didn't. C is ungrammatical. D misplaces 'almost.'

examples.q:
Which version correctly fixes the dangling modifier?

A) To qualify for the scholarship, a minimum GPA of 3.5 must be maintained.
B) To qualify for the scholarship, students must maintain a minimum GPA of 3.5.
C) A minimum GPA of 3.5 must be maintained in order to qualify for the scholarship.
D) Both B and C are correct.
examples.a:
Correct answer: D) D

A: 'To qualify for the scholarship' — who qualifies? The GPA doesn't qualify; students do. A has a dangling modifier. B fixes it correctly: students are the subject doing the qualifying. C restructures the sentence so the infinitive is no longer an opening modifier — also correct. D is the answer.

sessions.title: Parallel Structure
theory: PARALLEL STRUCTURE (parallelism) requires that words, phrases, or clauses in a series or comparison have the same grammatical form. When a sentence lists or compares items, all items must match in form: all nouns, all infinitives, all -ing phrases, all clauses, etc. 'She likes swimming, hiking, and to run' violates parallelism — mix of gerunds and infinitive. Correct: 'She likes swimming, hiking, and running' OR 'She likes to swim, to hike, and to run.' The SAT tests parallelism in lists (and/or), correlative conjunctions (both/and, either/or, not only/but also, neither/nor), and comparative structures.

CORRELATIVE CONJUNCTIONS require strict parallelism: whatever comes after the first conjunction must match grammatically with whatever comes after the second. 'Both working late AND to skip lunch' — wrong. 'Both working late AND skipping lunch' — correct (both are gerunds). 'Not only DID she win the competition BUT ALSO received a standing ovation' — wrong. 'Not only DID she win the competition BUT ALSO DID she receive a standing ovation' or 'Not only did she win but also receive...' The structures on both sides must match.

COMPARING LIKE WITH LIKE: parallelism also requires that comparisons be made between grammatically equivalent and logically comparable things. 'The climate in Norway is colder than Spain' — wrong (comparing climate to Spain). 'The climate in Norway is colder than the climate in Spain' or 'The climate in Norway is colder than Spain's.' 'She worked harder than her colleague did' or 'than her colleague.' Both comparing people's work. This type of error is especially common in academic writing on the SAT.
keys: All items in a series must have the same grammatical form
Gerunds: swimming, hiking, running (not 'to run')
Infinitives: to swim, to hike, to run (not 'running')
Correlatives: both X and Y | not only X but also Y | neither X nor Y
Both sides of correlative must match grammatically
Comparisons: compare LIKE with LIKE (climate to climate, not climate to country)
Fix: identify the pattern, then make all items match

examples.q: Which version is correctly parallel?
opts: The program requires reading, writing, and to solve mathematical problems.
The program requires reading, writing, and solving mathematical problems.
The program requires to read, writing, and solving mathematical problems.
The program requires reading, to write, and solving mathematical problems.
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) The program requires reading, writing, and solving mathematical problems.

B uses three gerunds: reading, writing, solving. All in the same -ing form. A mixes gerunds and an infinitive. C mixes infinitive and gerunds. D mixes gerund, infinitive, and gerund.

examples.q: Which version is correctly parallel?
opts: The new policy will not only reduce emissions but also improving air quality.
The new policy will not only reduce emissions but also improve air quality.
The new policy will not only reducing emissions but also improve air quality.
The new policy not only will reduce emissions but will also improving air quality.
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) The new policy will not only reduce emissions but also improve air quality.

'Not only X but also Y' — both sides must match. B: 'not only REDUCE (bare infinitive) but also IMPROVE (bare infinitive)' — parallel. A: 'reduce' (infinitive) vs. 'improving' (gerund) — not parallel. C: 'reducing' vs. 'improve' — not parallel. D is structurally awkward.

examples.q: Which version is correctly parallel?
opts: The study examined how poverty affects education, what happens to health outcomes, and the implications of housing instability.
The study examined how poverty affects education, how it affects health outcomes, and how housing instability creates long-term consequences.
The study examined how poverty affects education, health outcomes, and implications of housing instability.
The study examined the effects of poverty on education, health outcomes, and what housing instability does.
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) The study examined how poverty affects education, how it affects health outcomes, and how housing instability creates long-term consequences.

B: three parallel 'how' clauses — 'how poverty affects education / how it affects health outcomes / how housing instability creates consequences.' All three have the same structure. A mixes two 'how' clauses and a noun phrase. C is partially parallel. D mixes noun phrases and a clause.

examples.q: Which version makes a correct parallel comparison?
opts: The average salary of engineers in Germany is higher than France.
The average salary of engineers in Germany is higher than in France.
The average salary of engineers in Germany is higher than France's engineers.
The average salary of engineers in Germany is higher than the average salary of engineers in France.
examples.a:
Correct answer: D) The average salary of engineers in Germany is higher than the average salary of engineers in France.

D clearly compares 'average salary of engineers in Germany' with 'average salary of engineers in France' — salary to salary. B is also acceptable ('higher than in France' is idiomatic). A incorrectly compares salary to France (a country). C compares salary to 'France's engineers' (illogical). D is the most explicit.

examples.q: Which version correctly uses neither/nor?
opts: The report was neither thoroughly researched nor did it present its conclusions clearly.
The report was neither thoroughly researched nor clearly presented.
The report neither was thoroughly researched nor presenting its conclusions clearly.
Neither the research was thorough nor the conclusions clearly.
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) The report was neither thoroughly researched nor clearly presented.

B: 'neither THOROUGHLY RESEARCHED (adjective phrase) nor CLEARLY PRESENTED (adjective phrase)' — both are adjective phrases describing 'the report.' Parallel. A mixes adjective phrase and clause. C mixes 'was' and gerund. D is incomplete and awkward.

sessions.title: Verb Tense — Consistency & Sequence
theory: VERB TENSE tells the reader WHEN an action occurs. The SAT tests two main tense skills: (1) TENSE CONSISTENCY — don't shift tenses unnecessarily within a passage. If a passage describes historical events in the past tense, all verbs should stay in the past tense unless there is a clear reason to shift (e.g., describing a current truth vs. a historical event). 'Galileo observed the moons of Jupiter. He publishes his findings' — wrong shift from past to present. (2) TENSE SEQUENCE — when events happen at different times, verbs must reflect the correct time relationship using perfect tenses.

PERFECT TENSES: PAST PERFECT ('had + past participle') shows that one past action occurred BEFORE another past action. 'By the time the rescue team arrived, the survivors had built a shelter.' (building happened before arriving). PRESENT PERFECT ('have/has + past participle') shows a past action with present relevance, or an action that began in the past and continues. 'Scientists have discovered three new species this year.' FUTURE PERFECT ('will have + past participle') shows an action that will be complete before a future point. 'By 2050, renewables will have replaced most fossil fuels.'

COMMON TENSE ERRORS on the SAT: (1) Unnecessary tense shift mid-passage. (2) Using simple past when past perfect is needed to show prior occurrence. 'When the inspector arrived, someone already removed the evidence' — should be 'someone had already removed' (removal before arrival). (3) Mixing present and past in historical or narrative passages. Strategy: find the BASE TENSE of the passage. All verbs should be in that tense unless a time signal (before, after, already, by the time, since) requires a different tense.
keys: Tense consistency: establish base tense, stay in it throughout
Past perfect (had + PP): earlier past action before another past action
Present perfect (have/has + PP): past with present relevance, or ongoing since past
Signal words → past perfect: before, after, already, by the time, when (two past events)
Future perfect (will have + PP): completed before a future point
Present tense for CURRENT TRUTHS even in historical passages: 'Water freezes at 0°C'
Avoid: simple past when sequence requires past perfect

examples.q:
Which version maintains consistent tense?

Context: A passage about events in 1969.

A) Scientists monitored the mission closely. They track every signal from the spacecraft.
B) Scientists monitored the mission closely. They tracked every signal from the spacecraft.
C) Scientists monitor the mission closely. They tracked every signal from the spacecraft.
D) Scientists are monitoring the mission closely. They are tracking every signal from the spacecraft.
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) B

The passage describes 1969 — past tense. B uses past tense throughout: 'monitored...tracked.' A shifts to present ('track'). C shifts to present then back to past. D uses present progressive — wrong for historical events.

examples.t: Example 2 — Past Perfect for Prior Events
examples.q: Which version correctly shows that the evidence was removed BEFORE the inspector arrived?
opts: When the inspector arrived, someone already removed the evidence.
When the inspector arrived, someone had already removed the evidence.
When the inspector had arrived, someone already removed the evidence.
When the inspector arrived, someone has already removed the evidence.
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) When the inspector arrived, someone had already removed the evidence.

'Already removed' = happened before 'arrived.' For an earlier past event, use PAST PERFECT: 'had already removed.' B is correct. A uses simple past — doesn't show the sequence. C wrongly uses past perfect for arrival (the arrival isn't the earlier event). D uses present perfect — wrong tense entirely.

examples.t: Example 3 — Present Perfect vs. Simple Past
examples.q:
Which version correctly uses the present perfect?

Context: Current state of research.

A) Scientists discovered three new species of deep-sea bacteria in the past decade.
B) Scientists have discovered three new species of deep-sea bacteria in the past decade.
C) Scientists had discovered three new species of deep-sea bacteria in the past decade.
D) Scientists were discovering three new species of deep-sea bacteria in the past decade.
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) B

'In the past decade' — an ongoing period up to now — requires PRESENT PERFECT ('have discovered'). B is correct. A (simple past) is used for completed events at a specific time. C (past perfect) requires a reference point in the past. D (past progressive) suggests ongoing action in the past.

examples.t: Example 4 — Identifying the Error in Tense Sequence
examples.q:
Text: 'The archaeologists discovered that an ancient civilization occupied the site for centuries before mysteriously disappearing.'

Which is the error and how should it be fixed?
opts: 'discovered' should be 'had discovered'
'occupied' should be 'had occupied'
'disappearing' should be 'disappeared'
There is no error in this sentence.
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) 'occupied' should be 'had occupied'

The occupation and disappearance happened BEFORE the discovery. 'Occupied' should be 'had occupied' to show the occupation preceded the discovery. B is correct. 'Discovered' is the reference point in the past (simple past is fine). 'Disappearing' is a participial modifier — it can stay.

examples.q:
Text: 'By the time the infrastructure project is complete in 2028, engineers [___] over a decade on its design.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
opts: spend
spent
will spend
will have spent
examples.a:
Correct answer: D) will have spent

The time signal 'by the time [future point]' requires FUTURE PERFECT — an action completed before a specified future point. D: 'will have spent' correctly expresses that the spending will be completed by 2028. A (present) and B (past) are wrong tenses. C (simple future) doesn't convey the completion by 2028.

sessions.title: Subjunctive Mood & Conditional Structures
theory: MOOD refers to the form a verb takes to indicate the attitude toward the action. The INDICATIVE mood states facts ('She is a scientist'). The SUBJUNCTIVE mood expresses wishes, doubts, hypotheticals, recommendations, or conditions contrary to fact. The SAT tests two subjunctive patterns: (1) PRESENT SUBJUNCTIVE in 'that' clauses after verbs of recommendation, demand, suggestion, request, or requirement: 'The committee recommended that she PRESENT her findings' (not 'presents'). Always base form (no -s, no -ed, no -ing). Common triggers: recommend, suggest, require, demand, insist, propose, ask, request, urge.

PAST SUBJUNCTIVE for CONTRARY-TO-FACT conditions: use 'were' (not 'was') for all subjects. 'If I were president...' (not 'if I was') — this is a hypothetical, not a real condition. 'If she were taller...' 'If the data were complete...' 'As if he were an expert...' The test: is the condition FALSE or HYPOTHETICAL? If yes → 'were.' If the condition might be TRUE → use normal 'was.' 'If the report was accurate, we can proceed' (it might be accurate) vs. 'If the report were accurate, we could proceed' (it's not accurate — hypothetical).

CONDITIONAL STRUCTURES: 'If...would' patterns. Real/possible conditions use simple present + simple future: 'If she studies, she will pass.' Hypothetical conditions use past + would: 'If she studied, she would pass.' Contrary-to-fact past conditions use past perfect + would have: 'If she had studied, she would have passed.' The SAT error: mixing the conditional tiers. 'If she studies, she would pass' mixes real condition (present) with hypothetical result (would) — wrong. Match the tier consistently.
keys: Subjunctive: recommend/require/insist/suggest + that + SUBJECT + BASE VERB
'Recommend that she GO' (not 'goes') | 'Require that he BE' (not 'is')
Contrary-to-fact: 'If I WERE...' (not 'was') for all subjects
Real condition: If + present → will + base verb
Hypothetical: If + past → would + base verb
Contrary-to-fact past: If + past perfect → would have + past participle
Never: 'If she would study' — never 'would' in the 'if' clause

examples.q: Which version correctly uses the subjunctive?
opts: The board required that all members submits a disclosure form.
The board required that all members submit a disclosure form.
The board required that all members submitted a disclosure form.
The board required that all members are submitting a disclosure form.
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) The board required that all members submit a disclosure form.

'Required that' + SUBJECT + BASE VERB (subjunctive). B: 'submit' — base form, no -s. Correct. A uses third-person singular ('submits') — wrong in subjunctive. C uses past tense. D uses present progressive.

examples.q: Which version correctly uses the subjunctive?
opts: If the population was larger, the city would receive more federal funding.
If the population were larger, the city would receive more federal funding.
If the population would be larger, the city would receive more federal funding.
If the population has been larger, the city would receive more federal funding.
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) If the population were larger, the city would receive more federal funding.

'If the population were larger' is CONTRARY-TO-FACT (the population is NOT larger). Use 'were' for all subjects in hypothetical conditions. B is correct. A uses 'was' — acceptable in informal English but not the formal SAT standard. C uses 'would be' in the 'if' clause — never allowed. D uses present perfect — wrong.

examples.q: Which version best expresses a REAL/POSSIBLE condition?
opts: If the funding were approved, the research will begin next month.
If the funding is approved, the research will begin next month.
If the funding was approved, the research would begin next month.
If the funding would be approved, the research will begin next month.
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) If the funding is approved, the research will begin next month.

Real/possible condition (funding might be approved): 'If + present → will + base.' B: 'If the funding IS approved, the research WILL begin.' Correct. A mixes subjunctive 'were' with 'will' (hypothetical + real = inconsistent). C uses past tense (hypothetical). D uses 'would be' in the if-clause (never correct).

examples.q: Which version correctly expresses: the project failed because the team didn't plan properly — and the speaker is reflecting on what would have been different.
opts: If the team planned better, the project would succeed.
If the team had planned better, the project would have succeeded.
If the team were to plan better, the project will succeed.
If the team plans better, the project would have succeeded.
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) If the team had planned better, the project would have succeeded.

Contrary-to-fact PAST (the team DID NOT plan well, the project DID fail): use PAST PERFECT in 'if' clause + 'would have' in result. B: 'If they HAD planned...the project WOULD HAVE succeeded.' Correct. A is a hypothetical present-to-future (not past). C uses were-to + will (mixed). D mixes real condition (plans) with past result (would have succeeded).

examples.q: Which version correctly uses the subjunctive after a trigger verb?
opts: The professor suggested that the student revises her thesis.
The professor suggested that the student revised her thesis.
The professor suggested that the student revise her thesis.
The professor suggested that the student is revising her thesis.
examples.a:
Correct answer: C) The professor suggested that the student revise her thesis.

'Suggested that' + subjunctive: SUBJECT + BASE VERB. C: 'suggested that the student REVISE' — base form. Correct. A uses third-person 's' ('revises'). B uses past tense ('revised'). D uses present progressive.

sessions.title: Mixed Practice Strategy — Processing Question Types
theory: By Day 19, you have covered all major SAT Reading & Writing categories. The final days are about INTEGRATION — applying multiple skills quickly and accurately under timed conditions. The Digital SAT gives you approximately 71 seconds per question in Module 1 and slightly less in Module 2. This section reviews a critical meta-skill: IDENTIFYING THE QUESTION TYPE in 3 seconds, which allows you to apply the right strategy immediately. Question type determines strategy: don't use a 'meaning' strategy on a 'structure' question.

QUESTION TYPE IDENTIFICATION: (1) 'Which choice best states the main idea?' → Central claim strategy. (2) 'As used in the text, X most nearly means...' → Context substitution. (3) 'Which choice most logically completes the text?' → Transition/logical connection. (4) 'Which finding best supports the claim?' → Evidence matching. (5) 'Which choice conforms to Standard English conventions?' → Grammar rules. (6) 'Which choice most effectively accomplishes...' → Rhetorical purpose. (7) 'Based on the texts, both authors...' → Cross-text connection.

THE TWO-PASS STRATEGY for timed practice: on your first pass, answer every question you can complete confidently in under 90 seconds. Mark any question taking longer than 90 seconds and move on. On your second pass, return to marked questions with remaining time. Never spend 4+ minutes on a single question. On the Digital SAT, you can mark questions and return to them within the module. The second module is adaptive — your performance in Module 1 determines whether Module 2 is harder or easier.
keys: ~71 seconds per question on average (Digital SAT format)
Read the QUESTION STEM first — it tells you what to look for in the passage
For grammar: find the subject-verb, check tense, check agreement
For rhetoric: identify the paragraph's purpose BEFORE evaluating answer choices
For evidence: match the SPECIFIC claim, not just the general topic
Mark and move: never spend 4+ min on one question
Process of elimination: remove clearly wrong first, then choose best of remaining

examples.q: Which question type matches this stem: 'The main purpose of the second paragraph is to...'?
opts: Words in Context
Structure & Function
Evidence Support
Standard English Conventions
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) Structure & Function

'Main purpose of a paragraph' = Structure & Function question. Strategy: identify the paragraph's role in the argument (does it introduce, support, contrast, conclude, etc.?). B is correct.

examples.q:
Text: 'The report's findings, along with the recommendations of the expert panel, [___] to be reviewed by the full committee before any action is taken.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
opts: need
needs
needing
are needing
examples.a:
Correct answer: A) need

Step 1 (identify type): subject-verb agreement. Step 2 (find subject): cross out 'along with the recommendations of the expert panel' (intervening phrase). Subject = 'findings' (plural) → plural verb → 'need.' A is correct.

examples.q:
A student claims: 'Urban tree canopy directly reduces residents' heat exposure.'

Which finding best supports this specific claim?
A) Cities with more green space have higher property values.
B) Studies measuring surface temperatures find that tree-covered streets are 10-15°C cooler than treeless streets in summer.
C) Urban tree planting programs require significant municipal funding.
D) Many urban residents report preferring parks to concrete environments.
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) B

The claim is specifically about 'directly reduces heat exposure.' B provides the specific causal mechanism (tree canopy → cooler surfaces → reduced heat exposure) with quantified data. A is about property values (not heat). C is about funding. D is about preferences (not heat measurements).

examples.t: Example 4 — Rhetorical Purpose under Time Pressure
examples.q: A student is writing about the history of antibiotics. The paragraph currently ends with 'The discovery transformed medicine permanently.' Which sentence, if added next, would most effectively transition to a new paragraph about antibiotic resistance?
opts: Penicillin was discovered accidentally by Alexander Fleming in 1928.
However, this transformation carried an unintended consequence that only became apparent decades later.
Antibiotics are among the most commonly prescribed medications worldwide.
The pharmaceutical industry invested heavily in antibiotic development throughout the 20th century.
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) However, this transformation carried an unintended consequence that only became apparent decades later.

The transition must: (1) acknowledge the preceding claim (transformation), and (2) pivot to resistance (unintended consequence). B does both — 'this transformation' links to S1, and 'unintended consequence' sets up the resistance topic. A is background already established. C is a current fact, not a transition. D about investment doesn't lead to resistance.

examples.q:
Text: 'Scientists have [___] that elevated CO₂ levels cause coral bleaching, documenting measurable bleaching events following every major spike in atmospheric CO₂.'

Which best completes the text?
opts: theorized
speculated
demonstrated
guessed
examples.a:
Correct answer: C) demonstrated

The evidence is STRONG: 'documenting measurable bleaching events following every major spike' — this is repeated, correlated, quantified data. 'Demonstrated' = appropriate for strong, documented evidence. 'Theorized' and 'speculated' = appropriate for hypotheses without strong evidence. 'Guessed' is informal and implies no evidence at all. Eliminate D immediately, then A and B based on evidence strength. C remains.

sessions.title: High-Difficulty Questions — Traps & How to Beat Them
theory: The hardest SAT questions (difficulty 4-5) follow predictable TRAP PATTERNS. Knowing the traps prevents losing points to careless errors. Trap 1: ADJACENT ANSWER — an answer that is almost right, but slightly wrong in a crucial way. It uses the right vocabulary, the right topic, and the right structure — but either over-claims, under-claims, introduces something not in the text, or changes the emphasis. Always check the boundaries: does this answer say exactly what the text says, no more, no less?

Trap 2: TOO GENERAL or TOO SPECIFIC. For main idea questions, the correct answer captures the FULL SCOPE of the passage — not just one paragraph, and not a broader claim than the text supports. For evidence questions, the answer must match the SPECIFIC claim — not just the general topic. Trap 3: OPPOSITE DIRECTION — an answer that sounds plausible but actually argues the REVERSE of what the passage says. This trap is common in inference and implication questions where the passage is nuanced.

Trap 4 (Grammar): The CLOSEST NOUN trap in subject-verb agreement — choosing the verb to agree with the noun closest to it rather than the actual subject. Trap 5 (Rhetoric): The INTERESTING BUT IRRELEVANT trap — an answer that adds genuine information but doesn't serve the paragraph's specific function at that moment. Trap 6: EXTREME LANGUAGE — 'always,' 'never,' 'all,' 'none,' 'completely,' 'entirely' — the SAT rarely supports absolute claims, and answers with these words are usually wrong.
keys: Adjacent answer: right topic, right tone — but subtly wrong in scope or direction
Too general: broader than passage supports | Too specific: misses full scope
Opposite direction: especially dangerous in inference/implication questions
Closest noun trap: find the REAL subject, not just the closest noun
Interesting but irrelevant: passes the topic test but fails the purpose test
Extreme language: 'always/never/all/none' — almost always wrong on SAT
Final check: re-read the question stem after choosing — does your answer DO what was asked?

examples.t: Example 1 — Identifying the Adjacent Answer Trap
examples.q:
Passage: 'While most large language models struggle with complex logical reasoning, they excel at tasks involving pattern recognition and text generation. This asymmetry has led some researchers to argue that such models represent a fundamentally different kind of intelligence from human cognition.'

Which choice best states the main idea?
A) Large language models cannot reason logically.
B) Large language models are inferior to humans in all respects.
C) The uneven capabilities of large language models suggest they represent a form of intelligence qualitatively different from human intelligence.
D) Pattern recognition is the most important cognitive ability.
examples.a:
Correct answer: C) C

A is too specific — 'struggle' doesn't mean 'cannot.' B is too extreme ('all respects'). C captures the full argument: uneven capabilities + qualitatively different intelligence. D introduces a comparative judgment not in the passage. C is correct.

examples.q:
Passage: 'Critics of standardized testing argue that such tests measure test-taking skill as much as actual knowledge. Proponents counter that without standardized benchmarks, admissions decisions would rely even more heavily on subjective criteria that correlate more strongly with privilege than test scores do.'

Based on the passage, the proponents' argument implies that standardized tests
A) are a perfectly objective measure of student ability
B) may be imperfect but serve as a check against criteria that are even MORE correlated with privilege
C) are the primary cause of inequality in higher education admissions
D) should be weighted more heavily than subjective criteria in all admissions contexts
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) B

The proponents don't say tests are perfect — they say alternative criteria are 'even more' correlated with privilege. B captures this comparative argument. A overclaims (perfectly objective). C is the OPPOSITE of the argument — tests are defended against privilege concerns. D overclaims ('all contexts'). B is correct.

examples.q:
Passage: 'The 2008 financial crisis demonstrated that systemic risks within interconnected financial institutions can amplify local failures into global catastrophes. Specifically, the collapse of mortgage-backed securities triggered a chain reaction that reached financial systems in countries with no direct exposure to US housing markets.'

Which best states the central claim?
A) Financial markets are unstable and unpredictable.
B) The 2008 crisis was the worst financial crisis in history.
C) Interconnectedness in financial systems can allow localized failures to propagate globally, as demonstrated by the 2008 crisis.
D) Government regulation is needed to prevent future financial crises.
examples.a:
Correct answer: C) C

A is too general (all financial markets; the passage is about interconnectedness specifically). B is a comparison claim not made in the passage. C matches the argument precisely: interconnectedness → local to global propagation, with the specific 2008 example. D is a policy recommendation not made in the passage. C is correct.

examples.q:
Passage: 'Studies suggest that people who exercise regularly tend to report higher levels of life satisfaction on average. The correlation is robust across age groups and cultural contexts, though the causal mechanism is not fully established.'

Which inference is best supported?
A) Everyone who exercises regularly will experience greater life satisfaction.
B) Exercise is the most effective way to increase life satisfaction.
C) Regular exercise is consistently associated with higher self-reported life satisfaction, though causation has not been fully established.
D) People who report high life satisfaction always exercise regularly.
examples.a:
Correct answer: C) C

A: 'everyone' + 'will' = absolute, over-claims. B: 'most effective' requires a comparison not in the passage. C matches precisely: consistent association + causation not established. D: 'always' = absolute, reverse direction. C is correct.

examples.q:
Text: 'The impact of these three major regulatory changes on the competitive dynamics of the global telecommunications industry [___] been analyzed in several comprehensive studies.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
opts: have
has
having
are
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) has

Closest noun trap: 'industry' (singular) is closest to the verb — tempting you to choose 'has.' But the REAL SUBJECT is 'impact' (singular). Cross out 'of these three major regulatory changes on the competitive dynamics of the global telecommunications industry.' Subject = 'impact' (singular) → 'has.' B is correct.

sessions.title: Test-Day Strategy — Maximizing Your Score
theory: Day 20 is about STRATEGY — the habits and decisions that determine whether your knowledge translates into points. Strategy principle 1: ATTACK THE QUESTION, NOT THE PASSAGE. The SAT passage is a tool for answering specific questions. You don't need to fully comprehend every nuance before answering. Read enough to answer the question being asked, then move on. Strategy principle 2: ANCHOR EVERY ANSWER IN THE TEXT. Every correct answer to a Reading question is directly supported by specific words in the passage. If you can't point to specific language that supports your answer, choose a different answer.

Strategy principle 3: ELIMINATE SYSTEMATICALLY. On hard questions, eliminating two wrong answers often reveals the correct one. Wrong answers have identifiable flaws: too broad, too narrow, opposite direction, not in the passage, extreme language, or mixes true and false elements. Strategy principle 4: FOR GRAMMAR QUESTIONS, TRUST THE RULES. Don't choose an answer because it 'sounds right' — sounds right is how you learned informal English. The SAT tests formal written English. Apply the specific rule you've learned.

Strategy principle 5: MANAGE YOUR ADAPTIVE ADVANTAGE. The Digital SAT has two modules. Your Module 1 performance determines whether you get an easier or harder Module 2. A harder Module 2 means you can score higher — high scorers should aim for a harder Module 2. In Module 1: do not rush through early (easy) questions. Read carefully. The easy questions are where everyone scores points — losing one easy question to carelessness hurts more than missing one hard question.
keys: Attack the question: read what you need, not everything
Anchor answers in text: can you point to exact words that support it?
Wrong answer patterns: too broad, too narrow, opposite, not in text, extreme
Grammar: apply rules, don't rely on 'sounds right'
Module 1: careful on easy questions | Module 2: pace through medium, fight hard ones
Mark and return: don't spend 4+ min on any single question
Final 2 minutes: review marked questions, check no blanks remain

examples.q:
Passage: 'The 1930s Dust Bowl, while catastrophic in its immediate effects, prompted a lasting transformation in American agricultural policy. Federal programs established soil conservation practices that remain in use today, and the crisis catalyzed the understanding that land use was a national concern requiring federal oversight.'

Which inference is BEST supported by evidence in the passage?
opts: The Dust Bowl was the worst environmental disaster in American history.
The Dust Bowl led to lasting changes in both agricultural practice and policy.
Federal programs were ineffective in addressing the Dust Bowl.
The Dust Bowl demonstrated that individual farmers cannot be trusted.
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) The Dust Bowl led to lasting changes in both agricultural practice and policy.

B is directly supported: 'lasting transformation in agricultural policy' + 'soil conservation practices that remain in use today.' A requires a comparison not in the passage. C is directly contradicted. D is not stated. B is correct — and you can point to exact words.

examples.q:
Text: 'The enzyme catalyzes the reaction by lowering the activation energy required for the reaction to proceed, allowing it to occur at temperatures compatible with biological systems.'

As used in the text, 'compatible with' most nearly means:
opts: superior to
identical to
able to function within the conditions of
harmful to
examples.a:
Correct answer: C) able to function within the conditions of

Eliminate: A (superior) — the enzyme makes reactions possible at low temperatures; 'superior' misses the 'possible/compatible' relationship. B (identical) — the reaction doesn't need temperatures identical to biological systems. D (harmful) — opposite. C remains: 'able to function within the conditions of biological systems.' C is correct.

examples.q:
Text: 'Unlike most vitamins, vitamin D can be synthesized by the human body through exposure to sunlight.'

Which choice best states what distinguishes vitamin D from most other vitamins?
opts: It is found in dairy products.
It is important for bone health.
It can be produced by the body through sun exposure, unlike most vitamins.
It is the most commonly deficient vitamin worldwide.
examples.a:
Correct answer: C) It can be produced by the body through sun exposure, unlike most vitamins.

This is an easy Q1-level question. The passage says 'unlike most vitamins, vitamin D can be synthesized through sunlight.' C directly echoes this: produced by the body through sun exposure, unlike most vitamins. Don't overthink easy questions — anchor the answer directly in the text.

examples.t: Example 4 — Formal Written English vs. 'Sounds Right'
examples.q:
Text: 'The data, collected from ten research sites across three continents, [___] a consistent pattern of temperature increase over the past fifty years.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
opts: show
shows
are showing
have shown
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) shows

Many students choose 'show' because 'data' is plural in formal Latin usage. However, modern English increasingly treats 'data' as singular when referring to a body of information. More importantly: cross out the intervening phrase → 'The data ___ a consistent pattern' → in context, 'shows' (singular) is correct. B is correct. Trust the rules, not 'sounds right.'

examples.q:
You are taking Module 1 of the SAT R&W section. You are at Question 18 of 27, and Question 17 was a very hard inference question that took you 3 minutes. You have 25 minutes remaining. What is the optimal strategy?

A) Spend another 3 minutes on Question 18 since it's already hard
B) Mark Question 17 for review, continue to Question 18 with normal pacing, and return to Question 17 if time allows
C) Skip all remaining hard questions and only answer easy ones
D) Answer every question in exactly 71 seconds regardless of difficulty
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) B

B is the optimal strategy: mark difficult questions and continue. You have 25 minutes for 10 remaining questions (~2.5 min average), which is adequate. Never stop at one question for 4+ minutes — the points from later questions are equal. C leaves valuable points on the table. D is rigid and ignores question difficulty variation. B is correct.

sessions.title: Final Review — All 20 Rules in 20 Minutes
theory: This session consolidates the 20 most important rules across all 14 grammar and rhetoric days. GRAMMAR RULES: (1) Subject-verb: cross out intervening phrases, find the real subject. (2) 'The number' = singular; 'a number' = plural. (3) Collective nouns = singular (company, jury, team → its). (4) Or/Nor: match the closest subject. (5) Indefinite pronouns: each/everyone = singular; both/several = plural; all/some/none = depends. (6) Possessive pronouns: no apostrophe (its, their, whose). (7) 'It's' = it is; 'its' = possessive. (8) Who = subject; Whom = object. (9) Colon = must follow complete clause. (10) Semicolons require independent clauses on both sides.

GRAMMAR RULES (CONTINUED): (11) Comma splice = two independent clauses joined by comma alone. (12) Run-on = two clauses with no connector. (13) Fragment = missing subject or verb, or dependent clause alone. (14) Dangling modifier: opening phrase subject must match main clause subject. (15) Parallel structure: all items in a series must have the same form. (16) 'Not only X but also Y': both sides must match grammatically. (17) Subjunctive: recommend/require/suggest that + subject + BASE VERB. (18) Contrary-to-fact: 'If I WERE...' (not was). (19) Past perfect: use when one past event preceded another. (20) Verb tense: match the base tense of the passage; use perfect tenses for sequence.

RHETORIC RULES (TOP 10): (1) Main idea: covers FULL scope — not too narrow, not broader than passage. (2) Evidence: must match the SPECIFIC claim, not just the topic. (3) Inference: only what the text directly supports — don't add outside knowledge. (4) Transition: choose based on LOGICAL RELATIONSHIP, not just grammar. (5) Words in context: substitute and check meaning in context. (6) Purpose of sentence: what FUNCTION does it serve in the argument? (7) Add/Delete: serves the paragraph's specific purpose — not just related to the topic. (8) Placement: where content bridges are strongest. (9) Rhetorical synthesis: read the GOAL first, then find the choice that achieves it. (10) Word choice: match connotation, register, and precision to the passage's context.
keys: Grammar check order: agreement → tense → punctuation → modifier → pronoun
Rhetoric check order: question type → passage purpose → eliminate → verify
Evidence match: topic match ≠ claim match (must match the SPECIFIC claim)
Inference limit: only what the text says, nothing more
Transition: identify the relationship FIRST, then choose the signal
Word choice: formal/informal? Strong/hedged? Positive/negative connotation?
Every correct answer can be anchored in specific passage language

examples.q:
Text: 'The set of recommendations from the independent panel of advisors, which had been convened specifically to evaluate the policy's effectiveness, [___] that immediate reform was necessary.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
opts: suggest
suggests
are suggesting
have suggested
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) suggests

Multi-step check: (1) Find subject: cross out 'of recommendations from the independent panel of advisors' and 'which had been convened specifically to evaluate the policy's effectiveness.' Subject = 'The set' (singular). (2) Tense: past context → past tense. 'Suggested' would be correct — but none of the options is past. Current: 'suggests' (singular present) is the closest match. B is correct.

examples.q:
Passage: 'Urban food deserts — neighborhoods lacking access to affordable, nutritious food — are concentrated in low-income areas. Research shows that residents of food deserts have higher rates of diet-related illness than those in areas with good food access. Community-led initiatives, including mobile markets and cooperative grocery stores, have shown promise in addressing these gaps without requiring residents to travel long distances.'

Which sentence, if added, would most effectively conclude this paragraph?
opts: Food deserts are a well-documented phenomenon in American cities.
These community solutions suggest that addressing food access requires investment in local capacity rather than simply expecting market forces to fill the gap.
The USDA defines a food desert as a census tract with limited access to supermarkets.
Diet-related illness is a major public health concern in the United States.
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) These community solutions suggest that addressing food access requires investment in local capacity rather than simply expecting market forces to fill the gap.

The paragraph builds from problem → evidence → solutions. A conclusion should tie these together with a 'so what.' B does this: 'these community solutions' refers to the preceding examples, and 'local capacity rather than market forces' draws the policy implication. A and D are too general. C introduces a definition that doesn't conclude the argument. B is correct.

examples.t: Example 3 — Words in Context at Maximum Difficulty
examples.q:
Passage: 'The geopolitical landscape of the early 21st century has been characterized by the erosion of the multilateral institutions that provided the postwar liberal order with its structural coherence. Increasingly, bilateral and transactional relationships have supplanted the rule-governed frameworks that once constrained great power competition.'

As used in the text, 'supplanted' most nearly means:
opts: supplemented
replaced
criticized
supported
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) replaced

Substitute test: 'bilateral and transactional relationships have [___] rule-governed frameworks.' The passage describes an EROSION of multilateral institutions — things are being displaced, not added to. 'Supplanted' = replaced/displaced. B is correct. A (supplemented) = added to, not replaced. C and D don't fit.

examples.q:
Notes:
• Antarctic ice cores show CO₂ levels have increased from ~280 ppm (pre-industrial) to ~420 ppm (2023)
• Global average temperatures have increased ~1.1°C since pre-industrial times
• Ice core records show CO₂ and temperature changes have historically co-varied over 800,000 years
• Most climate scientists attribute current warming to human CO₂ emissions

A student wants to argue that current CO₂ increases are driving temperature rise consistent with historical patterns. Which synthesis best achieves this goal?
opts: CO₂ levels have risen from 280 to 420 ppm since pre-industrial times.

Ice core records spanning 800,000 years show that CO₂ and temperature have historically co-varied, providing a framework for understanding why the current 1.1°C warming correlates with the unprecedented rise in CO₂ from 280 to 420 ppm.
Global temperatures have increased by about 1.1°C since pre-industrial times.
Most climate scientists believe human activity is causing climate change.
examples.a:
Correct answer: B) Ice core records spanning 800,000 years show that CO₂ and temperature have historically co-varied, providing a framework for understanding why the current 1.1°C warming correlates with the unprecedented rise in CO₂ from 280 to 420 ppm.

The goal requires: current CO₂ increases + driving temperature rise + consistent with historical patterns. B combines all three: historical co-variation (pattern) + current CO₂ rise (280→420 ppm) + current temperature increase (1.1°C). A only gives CO₂ data. C only gives temperature data. D is about attribution without the specific mechanisms. B is correct.

examples.q: You encounter a question about the 'primary purpose of the third paragraph' in a passage you've read. You have 45 seconds left in your module, and you haven't looked at the third paragraph. What is the optimal approach?
opts: Skip the question and leave it blank
Re-read the entire passage from the beginning
Read ONLY the third paragraph (10-15 seconds), identify its role in the argument, select the best answer, and mark to review if needed
Guess and move on without reading anything
examples.a:
Correct answer: C) Read ONLY the third paragraph (10-15 seconds), identify its role in the argument, select the best answer, and mark to review if needed

C is optimal: targeted, efficient reading. You don't need to re-read the whole passage for a paragraph-purpose question — read the specific paragraph and identify its function. 45 seconds is enough for 10-15 seconds of reading + 15-20 seconds of evaluation. A wastes a point. B wastes 40+ seconds. D is better than A but worse than C. C is correct.
